articles.title: Zelensky Says Starlink Speeds Fully Restored, Urges Interceptor Deliveries
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 24, that SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite networks have had their operational speeds restored to pre-restriction levels, easing constraints that had affected counter-drone operations and front-line military logistics.
In a video address published on Telegram, the president confirmed that system diagnostics conducted by military specialists verified that bandwidth and velocity capabilities have returned to required operational thresholds.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The most important development for today: Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored to the speeds that existed prior to all these restrictions,” Zelensky stated.
“The restoration began overnight, and by this morning the speeds were already sufficient for operational use. This is very important and significant for our front-line logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
Zelensky confirmed that Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara delivered an official briefing on Saturday morning verifying that technical testing demonstrated full network functionality.
The president expressed gratitude to American partners, lawmakers, media, the US State Department, and US President Donald Trump for addressing the operational issue.
Appeals for ballistic interceptor deliveries
Addressing broader security cooperation with Western allies, Zelensky emphasized that Kyiv is maintaining active consultations with Washington and European partners to restore regular deliveries of surface-to-air interceptors capable of neutralizing Russian ballistic missiles.
Technocracy Takeover
The president noted that several critical air defense aid packages, backed by existing political approvals from partner nations, remain pending delivery to Ukrainian armed forces.
“We continue communicating with partners so that other levels of our cooperation with America are restored,” Zelensky said.
“It is very important that deliveries of air defense interceptors – interceptors against Russian ballistics – are renewed. There are packages that we are still awaiting. These include packages from America and from European partners – packages for which political decisions have already been adopted.”
The appeal follows Zelensky’s recent disclosures that Ukraine received only 24 Patriot interceptors from the US over the past three months, despite facing coordinated ballistic barrages and maintaining an estimated operational requirement of roughly 350 interceptors per month.
European diplomatic coordination and Oleshky humanitarian access
Zelensky disclosed that Ukrainian delegations are preparing a series of diplomatic consultations in Europe with representatives of the US president and European allies, emphasizing that European capitals must remain directly involved in all stages of prospective peace negotiations.
“Europe must be involved in the diplomatic process,” Zelensky stressed. “Ukraine always involves European partners in diplomatic efforts and counts on their continuation next week.”
The president also revealed that an agreement has been reached to secure humanitarian access to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Kherson region, where an estimated 1,700 civilians have faced acute isolation, hunger, and severed medical supplies.
Zelensky explained that Russian forces have heavily mined access roads leading to the left-bank enclave, creating critical survival hazards for remaining residents ahead of the winter season.
“There is also an agreement regarding Oleshky. Its implementation should take place soon so that access to Oleshky is unblocked,” Zelensky said.
“In the temporarily occupied part of our Kherson region, the Russians have mined roads, making the situation difficult – extremely difficult. We hope this humanitarian operation will succeed: unblocking Oleshky, providing access to deliver food and medicine, and allowing people to leave this combat zone.”
Zelensky confirmed that the humanitarian framework had been under discussion across multiple institutional levels, emphasizing that Ukraine will fulfill all operational commitments and counts on the effectiveness of American diplomatic mediation to secure the corridor.

articles.title: Iran says won’t allow US warships to get close as Trump ponders new attacks
articles.body:
Iran says won’t allow US warships to get close as Trump ponders new attacks
Iranian officials, media and analysts sense war is closer, but signal there will be no backing down.
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s armed forces say they are prepared to fire on United States warships as President Donald Trump said Washington was still deliberating new attacks or continued pressure on Iran.
Trump told supporters at a rally in Florida on Friday that the US military “may do another Epic Fury”, in reference to the extensive bombing campaign against Iran at the start of the war. He had earlier questioned whether to end the conflict quickly through huge attacks on Iran or let pressure on Tehran from a naval blockade and sanctions persist.
But Ali Abdollahi, chief of general staff of the Iranian armed forces, asserted that the US Navy is incapable of re-entering Iran’s territorial waters or its periphery due to Iran’s ability to target any vessel in the region.
“The US president can only dream of their soldiers and military again entering the Persian Gulf. They will take this wish to the grave for good,” he said in a statement carried by state media on Saturday morning.
Abdollahi also said US rhetoric about the war pointed to a basic contradiction: US claims that Iran’s military capabilities have been mostly destroyed during the war were nullified by its refusal to bring its aircraft carriers and support vessels closer to Iranian territory.
He added that Iranian forces were determined to “drown” the US and Israel in a “quagmire” in retaliation for their surprise attack on Iran on February 28, starting an eight-month war and plunging the whole region into instability.
Strait of Hormuz
Vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz continue to be attacked by Iran. Together with the increased odds of renewed war, this has driven up oil prices and sent Brent crude to its highest price since April, at about $117.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said seven tankers were attacked or hit mines overnight into Thursday. It then claimed on Friday that two supertankers struck mines. The IRGC has said its military doctrine is now more offensive, and Washington has reportedly ordered many diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia, with others set to depart other countries in the region.
The Iran-allied Houthis in Yemen also continued to exchange attacks with Saudi Arabia, hitting Riyadh again on Saturday, with the international airport in Dammam and the Shaybah oilfield targeted in recent days. Saudi forces have bombed Marib, Taiz and several other Yemeni provinces under Houthi control.
In southern Lebanon, Friday brought further reported Israeli air attacks around Nabatieh and artillery fire near Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah. Iran has linked this front to its war with the US and Israel, in the past demanding that any ceasefire with Washington also cover Lebanon.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing an election on October 27 which comes days before the November 3 mid-term elections in the US, also ordered a lockdown of the occupied West Bank after a Palestinian attack killed two soldiers in Hebron. The Houthis have also launched attacks on Israel linked to events in Gaza and the West Bank, highlighting how wider regional peace now depends on events in multiple theatres, including Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
Netanyahu has reiterated his desire to overthrow the Iranian government, leading several state-linked media and analysts in Iran to claim that Tehran has activated a “dead hand” doctrine. That allegedly enables military attacks against US, Israeli and regional interests to continue from across the country’s 31 provinces if senior Iranian figures are again assassinated as at the start of the war.
The IRGC has threatened seabed internet and communication cables if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is again targeted by the US and Israel. US-based Axios on Saturday cited US intelligence claiming that Iranian authorities had “substantially increased” efforts to strike American officials in the Middle East and beyond.
Diplomacy in Istanbul
Mediated negotiations between Iran and the US are no closer to yielding results. But regional and European powers held a coordination meeting in Istanbul on Friday and announced their expectations for the future of the war.
Top diplomats from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt met with the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy, with neither the US nor Iran participating.
“We agree that a new attack on Iran would widen the war and spread the conflict across the region,” Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said after the meeting. “Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one is endorsing it at this point.”
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said his government held Iran and the Houthis responsible for instability in the Middle East.
But the foreign ministers of the four regional countries issued a joint statement that said “Israeli occupation was the main source of instability in the region and beyond.”
In line with resolving the US-Israel war on Iran, the four regional countries supported the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed in June and a negotiated settlement, while demanding unrestricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz. The group said they opposed attacks on civilians and commercial vessels, and condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and its Red Sea shipping interests.
The Istanbul meeting once again displayed a “gap between diplomatic claims and realities in the field”, Nour News, an outlet affiliated with Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, argued in an analysis on Saturday.
It said the US and European powers – not Iran – must make concessions first. The outlet presented reopening the Strait of Hormuz as conditional on the US accepting Tehran’s demands and acknowledging responsibility for attacking Iran and Yemen.
Most Iranian newspapers on Saturday focused on signs of war, including rising oil prices.
The headline from hardline Vatan-e Emrooz reported that the price of a barrel of Brent crude rising above $117 was “evidence of disgrace for Trump”. Reformist Etemad said US and Israeli actions were signalling that the “zero hour” of another intense round of the war was approaching.
Reza Nasri, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst with links to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that after being subject to decades of attacks, nuclear sabotage, sanctions and violated deals by the US, Iran’s strategy was now “enough is enough.
“Iran has reached its verdict. It will no longer negotiate under bombardment, honour agreements the other side treats as optional, or accept the killing of its children and the penury of its people as routine instruments of policy,” he wrote on X. “It will put an end to this cycle, and it will do so by all necessary means”.

articles.title: Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government has said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.
The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.
The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.
The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need.”
The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.

articles.title: Russian air defenses down 1,297 drones over past 24 hours
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Russian air defense systems downed a SCALP air-launched cruise missile, four Neptune long-range cruise missiles, and 1,297 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.

The Ukrainian armed forces have lost approximately 1,190 troops over the past 24 hours as a result of actions by Russian armed forces in the special military operation zone, the Russian Defense Ministry reported. According to the ministry, the enemy lost over 200 personnel in the area of responsibility of the Battlegroup North, over 215 due to the actions of the Battlegroup West; up to 180 in the sector of the Battlegroup South, over 350 in the Battlegroup Center’s sector, over 205 in the area of responsibility of the Battlegroup East and up to 40 in the sector of the Battlegroup Dnepr.
Russian forces have struck energy and transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian military. "Operational-tactical aviation, attack drones, missile forces, and artillery of the Russian armed forces struck energy and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian military, as well as storage and launch sites for long-range unmanned aerial vehicles. Additionally, temporary deployment points for Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries were hit across 147 areas," the ministry said in a statement.

articles.title: Iran-backed militias in Iraq accuse US of violating airspace, as threats grow - analysis
articles.body:
Iran-backed militias in Iraq accused the United States of violating Iraqi airspace. The statement comes amid tensions between the Iraqi government and Iran-backed militias over efforts to bring weapons under state control, according to a report by Rudaw.
"Standing with the forces of righteousness against the forces of evil is a duty dictated by sound human nature," the IRI said, according to Rudaw. The group sees the conflict involving Iran as a struggle against the US and Israel. The IRI has attacked Israel in the past during the conflict in Gaza.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, continues to support Iran. The group issued a statement amid speculation about a possible new war with Iran.
The militias also accused Baghdad of appeasing the US due to Washington’s pressure on Iraq. The IRI is unhappy that Baghdad has been reducing commercial flights and closing border crossings with Iran. The IRI claimed to have documented 171 violations of Iraqi airspace by US fighter jets and reconnaissance aircraft between September 30 and Friday. The allegations were not independently verified.
The accusations come after the US-led anti-ISIS coalition formally ended its military mission in Iraq on September 30. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has sought to use the transition to bring militia weapons under government control. However, several powerful factions have rejected the initiative. The plan is set to take effect by June 2027. Some militias have agreed, while others have rejected the policy.
Some militias opposed to disarmament, others willing to cooperate
According to Rudaw, Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba remain opposed to disarmament, while Harakat Ansar Allah al-Awfiya and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have expressed willingness to cooperate with government measures.
Zaidi has extended the disarmament deadline to June 30, 2027, by which time "no weapons will remain outside the framework of the state," he said in an interview with Iraqi state media, quoted by Rudaw.
The dispute illustrates a central challenge facing Iraq. Even after the US-led coalition's withdrawal, Iran-backed factions continue to portray their weapons as necessary for confronting Washington and Israel. This puts them increasingly at odds with Baghdad's efforts to assert state authority over armed groups.
The tensions come as the US State Department has warned of increasing regional threats that could affect security in Iraq. On Saturday, the US Embassy in Iraq published an update to the State Department's travel advisory, citing the threat of increased attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis. The warnings also cite terrorist threats in Iraq, including those posed by Iran-backed militias.
The advisory maintained the existing warning against all travel to Iraq. It noted that Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure, could lead to wider regional escalation.
"The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area," the State Department warned. It also noted that "the Iraqi government cannot guarantee the safety of US citizens against sudden outbreaks of violence and armed conflict."
The advisory specifically highlighted threats from armed groups inside Iraq. "Terrorists, including ISIS and Iran-aligned militias, encourage and conduct attacks against US persons and interests in Iraq," the State Department said.
State Department warns of threats to US citizens, companies
It also warned that militias threaten American citizens and international companies, citing attacks involving drones, indirect fire, and improvised explosive devices. Potential targets include airports, energy infrastructure, hotels, and diplomatic facilities.
The warning illustrates the broader security challenges facing Baghdad. While the Iraqi government seeks to consolidate control over armed factions, Washington continues to view Iran-aligned militias as a threat. The escalation involving the Houthis also highlights how regional conflicts could further complicate Iraq's efforts to maintain stability and avoid being drawn into new confrontations.
The tensions in Iraq come amid other developments involving Iran and Iranian-backed groups across the region. On Saturday, Rudaw reported that US intelligence had warned of increased Iranian efforts to assassinate American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and elsewhere. Citing an Axios report, Rudaw said a memorandum dated Friday from US National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that some alleged Iranian plots had reached advanced stages. The report comes as Washington reduces staffing at several embassies amid concerns about regional escalation.
Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday that it had targeted a gathering center belonging to the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), an Iranian Kurdish opposition group. The attack took place in Iran but could have implications for Iraq, where Tehran has previously targeted Iranian Kurdish opposition groups. According to Rudaw, clashes between the IRGC and PJAK's armed wing, the Eastern Kurdistan Units (YRK), have intensified over the last week. Iran has used drones and artillery against mountainous areas where the Kurdish fighters operate. Iran's Mehr News Agency described the latest operation as a preemptive strike against PJAK members allegedly preparing attacks.
These developments also come as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi continues to insist that his government will end the presence of armed factions operating outside state control. In an interview quoted by Rudaw on Friday, Zaidi said that "Iraq will soon, God willing, be a state free of factions, like other countries in the world, and weapons will be exclusively in the hands of the Iraqi security forces."
The developments illustrate the competing pressures facing Iraq. Baghdad wants to consolidate state authority over armed groups, but Iran-backed militias continue to see themselves as part of a wider regional confrontation with the US and Israel. At the same time, Iran's operations against Kurdish opposition groups and reports of threats to American officials suggest that tensions could spread across several fronts.
One example of Baghdad's progress is a new agreement with a Yazidi armed group called YBS in Sinjar in northern Iraq. Baghdad also says it has reached a deal with Turkey for Ankara to leave a base near Bashiqa. However, these may be low-hanging fruit because Iran-backed militias are, in some ways, more powerful. Iran shares a long border with Iraq. It views Iraq as a "near abroad," basically meaning it feels it should control Iraq. It has carried out 1,000 attacks on the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, but also 600 on the rest of Iraq, using militias in some attacks.
For Iraq, the challenge is not only disarming militias. It is also preventing the country from becoming a battleground in a wider regional conflict. The coming months will test whether Zaidi can turn his government's commitments into reality, particularly as the June 2027 deadline approaches.

articles.title: Iran’s new military doctrine is designed to make victory meaningless
articles.body:
Iran’s latest military doctrine rests on a dangerous proposition: a country does not have to defeat a superior enemy on the battlefield to deny it a meaningful victory. By threatening broader retaliation, expanding the geography of conflict and exploiting vulnerabilities in regional trade, Tehran is attempting to make the political rewards of military action increasingly difficult to secure.
On Oct. 21, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that Iran’s military doctrine would move beyond retaliatory strikes towards offensive and asymmetric operations.
The declaration reinforced earlier statements by Iranian military officials that the country was shifting away from a predominantly defensive posture.
Although official announcements do not establish how comprehensively this change has been implemented, they reveal the direction in which Tehran wants its adversaries to believe its strategy is moving.
The distinction matters because military superiority and strategic success are not interchangeable. Washington and Israel may destroy military facilities, disrupt command structures and degrade Iran’s weapons production. Yet these achievements cannot, by themselves, guarantee political compliance, regional stability or a durable settlement.
Iran’s objective, therefore, is not necessarily to win a conventional war against the United States. Rather, it is to deny Washington the ability to translate battlefield superiority into a political outcome that Tehran considers unacceptable.
This strategy could raise the costs of another attack, but it could also deepen the insecurity that makes another war possible. The central question is no longer simply who can inflict greater damage. It is whether either side can turn military force into a political settlement that lasts.
What It Means to Win a War
Iran’s strategic predicament is straightforward. Its conventional air power and technological capabilities cannot match those of the United States and Israel. A strategy built around symmetrical warfare would leave Tehran vulnerable to sustained aerial attacks, precision strikes and the systematic destruction of military infrastructure. Its response has consequently relied on a different calculation: if it cannot prevent an adversary from striking, it can make the consequences of that strike more costly and unpredictable.
Missiles, drones, dispersed launch systems and decentralised command structures are central to this approach. Rather than depending exclusively on the survival of major military installations, Iran can seek to preserve enough capacity to retaliate after suffering substantial damage. Its longstanding emphasis on asymmetric warfare also allows it to exploit the difference between the relatively low cost of some offensive systems and the expense of intercepting them.
The strategic logic extends beyond weapons. Iran can threaten military facilities, shipping routes and economic infrastructure across a wider regional theatre.
A conflict that begins with strikes on Iranian territory could therefore create security and economic consequences for states that are not directly involved in the initial attack.
The threat of escalation becomes part of Iran’s deterrent, even before every threatened operation is carried out.
This is a strategy of strategic denial. Its purpose is not necessarily to defeat an opponent in every engagement but to prevent that opponent from achieving its political objectives at an acceptable cost. If Washington seeks to eliminate a military threat, compel Iranian concessions or reshape Tehran’s regional behaviour, the relevant measure of success is not simply the number of targets destroyed. It is whether the intended political outcome follows.
Yet strategic denial should not be confused with victory. A state that survives an attack may still lose military capacity, economic resources and diplomatic leverage. Iran’s ability to impose costs does not automatically give it the ability to dictate the terms of a settlement. Its doctrine may complicate an adversary’s calculations without resolving the underlying imbalance of power.
Beyond Iran’s Borders
The most consequential feature of Iran’s approach is its potential to widen the conflict geographically. Tehran does not need to confine its response to the immediate battlefield if it believes that pressure on regional infrastructure and international commerce can influence an adversary’s decisions. This creates a direct connection between military strategy and the global economy.
The Strait of Hormuz illustrates the problem. The US Energy Information Administration estimated that roughly 20 million barrels of oil per day passed through the strait in 2024, equivalent to about one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption. The route is also critical to international liquefied natural gas trade.
Any sustained disruption could increase energy prices, raise shipping and insurance costs, and intensify inflationary pressure across economies far beyond the Middle East.
For Iran, the strategic attraction is clear. A threat to a vital maritime chokepoint can make the consequences of military escalation visible to governments, businesses and consumers around the world. The resulting economic pressure may complicate the calculations of states supporting military action against Tehran. It also forces regional governments to consider whether hosting foreign military forces could expose their own economies to retaliation.
But this leverage has limits. Disrupting the Strait of Hormuz would also damage Iran’s interests, aggravate economic hardship and alienate states that might otherwise favour diplomacy. Other countries could respond by strengthening maritime coalitions, expanding alternative supply arrangements or increasing military pressure on Iran. A tactic designed to internationalise the cost of war could therefore internationalise the opposition to Tehran.
Nor does economic pain necessarily translate into political concessions. Governments may absorb substantial costs if they believe their security or credibility is at stake. The assumption that higher energy prices or disrupted trade will compel Washington to retreat is no more reliable than the assumption that military strikes will automatically force Tehran to comply.
Iran’s widening battlefield is thus both a source of leverage and a mechanism of escalation. It raises the stakes for all parties, but it also increases the number of actors with reasons to intervene. The more regional commerce becomes an instrument of coercion, the harder it becomes to separate military confrontation from the wider economic order.
Why Strategic Denial Is Not the Same as Victory
Iran’s doctrine may be designed to make an adversary’s victory elusive, but it cannot guarantee that Tehran will emerge in a stronger position. The strategy depends on the credibility of its threats, the survival of enough military capability to carry them out and the willingness of its opponents to consider the potential costs before acting. Each condition can change during a conflict.
A sustained campaign could weaken Iran’s missile infrastructure, reduce its stockpiles and disrupt the command systems needed to coordinate retaliation. Regional partners could also become less willing or less capable of supporting Tehran if the costs of confrontation rise. Meanwhile, attacks on neighbouring states or commercial shipping could encourage closer security cooperation between Gulf governments, Washington and other external powers.
There is also a fundamental political problem. A doctrine built around imposing unacceptable costs can deter an adversary, but it can also reinforce the adversary’s belief that Iran must be contained through stronger military pressure.
If every attack is answered by a wider threat and every response produces another escalation, the logic of deterrence risks becoming a cycle of mutual insecurity.
This is where Iran’s strategic calculation becomes especially precarious. Preventing an opponent from claiming victory is a negative objective. It can obstruct an adversary’s plans, but it does not establish a stable political order or secure long-term economic recovery. For Tehran, a meaningful strategic outcome would require more than surviving a confrontation. It would require preserving national security, reducing the risk of renewed war and creating conditions in which economic reconstruction becomes possible.
The same distinction applies to Washington and Israel. Tactical success may weaken Iran’s military capabilities, but it cannot by itself resolve the political disputes that sustain the confrontation. If military action leaves both sides convinced that the other remains an intolerable threat, battlefield gains may simply postpone the next round of conflict.
A more durable outcome requires a credible path from deterrence to diplomacy. Crisis communication channels, arrangements to protect commercial shipping and verifiable agreements on the issues driving confrontation would not eliminate the rivalry. They could, however, reduce the risk that a local incident triggers a broader regional war. Such mechanisms matter precisely because neither side can reliably control every consequence of escalation.
Iran’s new doctrine should therefore be understood not as proof that Tehran can defeat a militarily superior opponent, but as an effort to make the exercise of that superiority politically and economically costly. Its success will depend on whether the threat of retaliation changes adversarial behaviour without provoking a response that leaves Iran more isolated and vulnerable.
Ultimately, the measure of success is not whether an adversary can be prevented from claiming victory. It is whether either side can achieve a political settlement that remains viable after the guns fall silent.
A doctrine that makes victory elusive may deter aggression. Without a credible path to peace, however, it can also make the next war harder to avoid.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: US senators threaten to block Trump's nominees over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – NYT
articles.body:
US senators threaten to block Trump's nominees over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – NYT
US senators have warned the White House they will withhold their votes to confirm nominees until US President Donald Trump's administration secures the restoration of communications systems used by Ukrainian forces, The New York Times reports.
Source: The New York Times, citing sources
Details: According to three people familiar with the discussions, Republicans and Democrats in the Senate have told senior White House officials that they will block confirmation of Trump's nominees awaiting congressional approval until the administration restores critically important satellite communications capabilities used by the Ukrainian military.
The move, disclosed to the NYT by sources speaking on condition of anonymity because it has not yet been officially announced, will intensify bipartisan tensions over the White House's ever-more conciliatory approach towards Russia.
This will take place during the remaining congressional session scheduled for after the midterm elections, when Republicans are expected to try to confirm dozens of Trump's nominees before the current Congress's term ends.
The stance highlights growing divisions between the White House and Congress over Russia, with even senior Republicans showing increasing willingness to challenge Trump's policy positions. It also points to a possible shift after the midterm elections, when control of Congress could pass to the Democrats and lawmakers from both parties may be more resolute in using their leverage and oversight powers on the issue.
Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania who is fighting to retain his seat in a highly contested district, has threatened to seek the dismissal of US officials responsible for the network disruptions as well as cuts to their departments' budgets. He said he doubts the problems were accidental.
A US Senate staff member told the NYT on condition of anonymity that the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations had approved several shipments of critical air defence interceptors that had still not been delivered to Ukraine, raising concerns about delays in aid already authorised by Congress.
Staff are also considering launching investigations into SpaceX in connection with the satellite disruptions and have asked companies involved in Russian diesel fuel transactions to retain documents in the event of possible congressional investigations, the source added.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on President Donald Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike Russian targets 2,500 kilometers from border
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukraine struck several targets, including a petrochemical plant and a warehouse in Siberia around 2,500 kilometers away from the border on Oct. 24, monitoring channels reported.
A fire first broke out at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus.
The facility is one of Russia's largest petrochemical plants, and the company behind Omsky Kauchuk says the site is a leading producer of synthetic rubber, organic synthesis products, and methyl tert-butyl ether, an additive used to refine gasoline.
The plant is part of Russia's supply chain for rocket fuel, including for the Iskander ballistic missile used in fatal attacks against Ukraine, Exilenova Plus said.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a fatal attack on the night of Oct. 13-14, killing five people and injuring another 25.
Later, a warehouse belonging to major Russian online retailer Ozon was also hit in the Ukrainian drone attack, Exilenova Plus reported.
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaliy Khotsenko confirmed that the region was targeted by Ukrainian drones, saying that a logistics hub in the city of Omsk was hit.
"A logistics hub in Omsk was attacked by a drone. Personnel were promptly evacuated. Emergency services are working at the scene," he claimed.
Reports could not be immediately verified by the Kyiv Independent.
Ozon and its competitor Wildberries have been targeted by Ukrainian forces in recent months. The two are a major part of Russia's economy, with their broader ecosystems accounting for about 8.5% of Russia's GDP.
Ukraine has targeted facilities that often serve as storage sites for dual-use goods used in weapons production and other military purposes.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Omsk Oblast was also under fire in an attack on Oct. 8. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck the Omsk oil refinery.
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," Ukraine's General Staff said.
More recently, on Oct. 24, the General Staff said that Ukrainian forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, as well as an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai.
The synthetic rubbers are used to make solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles, according to the General Staff.
"Damage to such objects affects the supply chain of raw materials for the Russian missile program," Ukraine's General Staff wrote.

articles.title: Silence about attacks on nuclear facilities is unforgivable
articles.body:
Silence about attacks on nuclear facilities is unforgivable
Jam-e-Jam criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its response to attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities. The article argued that military strikes carried out by the United States and Israel against Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious violations of international law and the prohibition on aggression.
According to the paper, both the governing bodies and the Secretariat of the IAEA failed to issue even a statement condemning these actions, a situation unprecedented in the agency’s history. The newspaper claimed this failure exposed a major institutional weakness and raised concerns about the consistent application of principles that the agency is supposed to uphold. It argued that the IAEA cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks on safeguarded facilities as a secondary concern. Therefore, the agency should clearly reaffirm that attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities are unlawful, unacceptable, and should never be tolerated under any circumstances.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: Decoding an Emirati flight to Tehran
Donya-e-Eqtesad examined the repeated landing of an Emirati aircraft in Tehran. These flights sparked speculation about possible contacts between the UAE and Iran ahead of a potential new phase of regional tensions. The visits occurred at a time of intensified diplomatic activity across the region. The newspaper also noted that Trump’s support for Netanyahu before Israel’s national elections increased concerns about possible new attacks against Iran. Since the UAE aligned itself with the United States and Israel after the outbreak of conflict and was reportedly targeted by Iranian retaliatory actions, the return of a government-linked Emirati aircraft to Tehran attracted attention. Combined with earlier reports regarding possible arrangements related to frozen Iranian assets, the flights fueled speculation about behind-the-scenes communication between the two countries. Nevertheless, the true purpose of the flights remains unclear, leaving open the question of whether they were intended to ease tensions or serve another mission.
Ettelaat: E3’s proposal for mediation amid tensions
Ettelaat discussed the announcement by Germany, France, and the United Kingdom (known as European trio) that they are prepared to act as mediators between Tehran and Washington over the Iran nuclear issue. According to the newspaper, these three countries possess extensive experience in talks concerning Iran’s nuclear program and have long participated in diplomatic efforts aimed at ensuring its peaceful nature. The European initiative remains focused on preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, a goal that Berlin, Paris, and London continue to regard as essential for reducing regional tensions. European governments are therefore seeking to keep the door open for negotiations while responding to the rapidly evolving security situation in the Middle East. At the same time, Iran’s response to the proposal remains uncertain. Since the European troika has largely been sidelined in recent phases of the nuclear dispute, it remains to be seen whether Iran and the United States will once again bring these countries back into the negotiating process.
Etemad: Washington’s messages not genuine diplomatic initiatives
Etemad interviewed former Iranian parliamentarian Heshmatollah 
 
Falahatpisheh about the likelihood of war versus successful negotiations. While diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions continue, assessments of potential Iran-US talks remain cautious. Falahatpisheh argued that Washington’s recent messages are not genuine diplomatic initiatives but rather ultimatums containing strict demands. He believes the United States seeks to restrict significant parts of Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities, and that its proposals appear closer to demands for surrender than a basis for agreement. At the same time, he noted that Iran is trying to highlight the costs and vulnerabilities of any military confrontation, taking into account both US electoral considerations and Iran’s military posture. In his view, this strategy can strengthen deterrence while keeping diplomatic channels open.
Javan: No violations in the Strait of Hormuz
In an article, Javan addressed developments in the Strait of Hormuz. Contrary to misleading narratives from Trump and CENTCOM, field reports indicate that vessels involved in oil smuggling or other violations have reduced or halted their activities. The newspaper suggested that military measures and restrictions may be influencing maritime calculations in this strategic waterway. Meanwhile, rising oil prices, with crude exceeding $117 per barrel, demonstrated that developments in the Strait of Hormuz are not merely military issues but also have immediate consequences for global energy markets and the international economy. In this context, warnings from the IRGC Navy about expanding responses to US actions, alongside statements from the speaker of Parliament regarding the costs of conflict with Iran, reflected two complementary messages: Iran’s ability to affect one of the world’s most important energy corridors and a warning about the broader economic and strategic consequences of escalating tensions.

articles.title: Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
articles.body:
Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
US intelligence memo warns that Iranian plots against US citizens in the Middle East ‘have reached advanced stages’.
United States intelligence agencies have warned that Iran is in “advanced stages” of plans to target US personnel abroad, prompting Washington to place staff on high alert in the Middle East, according to US officials and an official memo cited by Axios and The New York Times (NYT).
The alert comes as the US and Israel signal they may be preparing for a new military campaign against Iran, which Tehran has reportedly threatened to retaliate against, in part by targeting communications cables in the Gulf.
The heightened threat assessment has prompted Washington, already on guard over escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthis, to trim Washington’s diplomatic presence in the Middle East, the NYT has reported, citing officials.
Here’s what we know about the latest US warning, and how it fits into the broader US-Iran conflict:
What has the US said about Iran’s alleged plans to attack Americans?
A warning about Iranian plans to target US citizens was detailed in a memo sent by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, first reported by US news site Axios.
In the memo, Clayton wrote that US agencies had received intelligence indicating that Iran has “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” overseas, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and other countries.
The NYT, which also reported on the memo, cited unnamed US officials as saying threats to American officials, including ambassadors, had been assessed in recent weeks, and that Iran had lined up potential targets in Europe.
The officials said some intelligence indicates Iranian operatives are already active within the US.
What evidence has Washington presented, and what remains unverified?
Washington has not publicly commented on the memo, although the NYT cited a US official as confirming its authenticity on behalf of President Donald Trump’s administration.
Another official cited by the NYT played down Iran’s ability to execute attacks inside the US and elsewhere, saying it lacks the capacity to follow through on all its ambitions.
Why have US officials raised the alarm now?
According to officials cited by the NYT, US agencies deem Iranian threats to US citizens in the Middle East to be “at the highest level” since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.
This assessment is behind the US’s recent moves to withdraw staff posted in the region, the NYT added.
In the background are reported US and Israel plans to initiate a new military campaign against Iran following the US mid-term elections next month. On Friday, Trump said the US “may do another little epic fury”, using the codename for the US-Israel war against Iran that began on February 28.
Which countries has the US withdrawn diplomats from?
On Wednesday, the US Department of State announced it was removing non-essential staff in its embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing escalating attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen against Saudi infrastructure.
Staff levels have also been quietly reduced at other US diplomatic missions in the region, several US media have reported. That includes embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Lebanon, according to CNN.
A US official cited by the NYT said the threat of Houthi attacks and “Iranian terror plots targeting US officials” were driving US staffing decisions.
Has Iran responded?
Iran has not responded to news of the US intelligence memo accusing it of planning attacks on US personnel.
However, Iranian officials have repeatedly threatened and carried out attacks against US bases and those of its allies in the region. The Pentagon has confirmed that 21 US military personnel have been killed in the Middle East since the war on Iran began.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that Tehran would follow a new “offensive” strategy if the US renewed attacks.
That means Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes, said IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi, adding that the quality, range and power of Iranian missiles had improved.
Tehran also has in-depth plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of new US-Israeli attacks, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two senior Iranian security officials.
Previously, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities across the region could come under attack if war with the US breaks out again.
Has Iran previously been accused of plotting attacks against Americans?
Yes, US authorities have long accused Iran of being behind plots targeting US citizens, including assassination attempts against Trump on US soil.
In March this year, a Pakistani national was convicted by a US court of plotting to assassinate Trump and other US politicians on the orders of Iran’s IRGC.
An Iranian IRGC member was charged in 2022 with trying to assassinate former US National Security Advisor John Bolton. The individual allegedly “attempted to pay individuals in the United States $300,000 to carry out the murder in Washington DC or Maryland”, according to the US Department of Justice.
Last year, the US intelligence community warned that Iran would “continue to directly threaten US persons globally”, specifically targeting officials it believed were involved in the 2020 assassination of IRGC Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani.
This month, the US abruptly withdrew bombers from an airbase in England, United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack. That followed a security incident at the base, after which the UK arrested several men on suspicion of working with Iranian intelligence.

articles.title: Protector drone flight over Channel was not for Home Office
articles.body:
An RAF Protector RG-1 that flew over the English Channel on 14 October was operating in support of defence aims and not in support of the Home Office, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, had asked for what reason the aircraft was tasked to support the Home Office in the Channel on that date.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Ministry of Defence regularly and routinely monitors our waters to protect UK interests, contribute to domestic maritime security, and act as a deterrent against potentially malign activities.
“The deployment the hon. Member refers to was conducted in support of Defence aims, not in support of the Home Office.”
Protector RG-1 is the RAF’s version of the General Atomics MQ-9B SkyGuardian, and the United Kingdom has ordered sixteen of them to replace the MQ-9A Reaper fleet that was retired after two decades of operations over Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria. The aircraft has a wingspan of around twenty four metres, an endurance of more than thirty hours and a maximum altitude above forty thousand feet, and carries Brimstone 3 missiles and Paveway IV bombs alongside its electro-optical and infrared sensors and a maritime search radar.
The aircraft is built to a NATO airworthiness standard and fitted with a detect and avoid system, lightning protection and de-icing, and that certification allows it to fly in unsegregated British airspace alongside civil traffic without a reserved block of sky being set aside for it. The Reaper it replaced could not, and needed segregated airspace or a danger area for every domestic sortie. The fleet is based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire with 31 Squadron, and operations are flown from ground control stations on the station.
Surveillance of small boat crossings in the Channel has been contracted out by the Home Office to a commercial operator. The Portuguese company Tekever has operated its AR5 maritime surveillance aircraft over the Channel since 2020 under Home Office contracts, a framework worth up to £1 billion and renewed repeatedly since. The AR5 is a twin-engine fixed-wing aircraft that flies for more than twelve hours and carries maritime and synthetic aperture radars, day and night cameras and receivers for vessel identification and distress beacons.
Paul Webb, managing director of Tekever UK, has said of the work that “drones can identify humans in distress in a much faster way and help rescue teams.” The company has since sold the same system to the Portuguese government and has expanded into supplying uncrewed aircraft to Ukraine.

articles.title: US taxpayer money laundered back through Ukraine – Musk
articles.body:
US taxpayer money laundered back through Ukraine – Musk
Billionaire Elon Musk has accused US politicians of putting Kiev’s interests ahead of their own country’s, alleging that American taxpayer money sent to Ukraine is being laundered back into political campaigns.
Writing on X on Friday, the SpaceX founder suggested that financial interests could explain why some American lawmakers remain staunch supporters of Kiev in its conflict with Russia.
“Some of that US taxpayer money comes back through multiple laundry machines to fund political campaigns in America, which is why you see some politicians caring more about Ukraine than America!” Musk wrote, without identifying the beneficiaries.
And some of that US taxpayer money comes back through multiple laundry machines to fund political campaigns in America, which is why you see some politicians caring more about Ukraine than America!
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 23, 2026
In March, US outlet Just the News cited a declassified intelligence summary describing a plan to divert hundreds of millions of dollars in American aid earmarked for clean-energy projects in Ukraine into then-President Joe Biden’s 2024 reelection campaign.
Trump shared the report on Truth Social, while then-US intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard reportedly asked officials at the US Agency for International Development (USAID) to investigate whether the alleged scheme had been carried out.
Musk also accused Ukrainian elites of profiting from Western assistance while ordinary Ukrainians bear the human cost.
“The former have grown very rich off the hundreds of billions flowing to Ukraine, while the latter’s children are conscripted to die in trenches,” he wrote.
Kiev’s increasingly coercive mobilization campaign has been marked by numerous documented cases of forced detentions and violent confrontations involving recruitment officers. Corruption investigations have also exposed schemes allowing wealthier Ukrainians to evade military service.
Ukraine has been rocked by major corruption scandals involving figures close to Vladimir Zelensky. One centered on his longtime associate Timur Mindich and an alleged $100 million bribery and money-laundering operation at state nuclear energy company Energoatom. The scandal forced senior officials from office, including former presidential chief of staff Andrey Yermak, while Mindich fled Ukraine.
Ukrainian investigators have also uncovered what they say is fraud to the tune of $5.6 million involving military drones purchased at prices up to 90% above market rates.
Even Kiev’s staunchest European backers have criticized its failure to deliver promised anti-corruption reforms, warning that billions of euros in assistance could be withheld.
Zelensky is seeking at least €70 billion ($81 billion) in additional foreign assistance for 2027, estimating Ukraine’s total conflict-related spending needs for next year at €155 billion.
European Council President Antonio Costa said on Friday that the EU expects to cover roughly two-thirds of the additional funding, or around €46.7 billion, with a decision potentially coming in November. That sum would come on top of the €45 billion already earmarked for Kiev next year.

articles.title: US updates Israel travel warning, cites growing threat from Iran-backed Houthis
articles.body:
The US State Department issued an updated travel advisory notice for Israel on Friday, warning of an increased threat of armed attacks by Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and the potential for a rapid escalation of regional hostilities.
The update did not change Israel's overall travel advisory classification, which remains at Level 3, urging American citizens to reconsider travel due to terrorism and unrest. The existing risk indicators and restrictions on travel to certain areas of the country also remain unchanged.
In its warning on armed conflict, the State Department cited previous Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure that resulted in civilian casualties and major travel disruptions.
The department warned that hostilities involving the Houthis could escalate rapidly beyond the areas immediately affected, potentially posing additional risks to travelers across the region.
The updated warning comes against the backdrop of previous missile threats originating from Yemen, which have required Israel to activate air defense systems and issue civilian alerts.
US maintains restrictions on travel to Israeli border areas
Despite the updated regional threat assessment, Washington has not raised its overall warning level for Israel. The State Department continues to advise Americans to reconsider travel because of terrorism and unrest, while maintaining stricter Level 4 restrictions in several designated areas.
These restrictions cover areas north of the Route 85, Route 90, and Route 87 boundaries in northern Israel; locations within 11.3 kilometers of the Gaza Strip; and areas within 2.4 kilometers of the Israel-Egypt border, except near the Taba crossing, also known as the Menachem Begin crossing.
The State Department said Israeli authorities restrict travel in the designated northern areas because of IDF activity and presence, and instructed Americans not to travel there for any reason.
US government employees working in Israel face the same geographical restrictions. Official travel to these areas requires approval from the US Embassy's security office.
The advisory also reiterated that, as of August 26, family members are permitted to accompany US government employees stationed in Israel. However, Washington warned that additional security measures affecting US personnel could be introduced as conditions evolve.
The State Department emphasized that Israel's security environment remains complex and can change rapidly, warning that violence could occur without advance notice.
Regional tensions could also prompt airlines to cancel flights or reduce services to and from Israel, potentially disrupting travel plans even in areas not subject to the highest-level restrictions.
Americans urged to prepare for missile and drone threats
The advisory urged American citizens planning to visit Israel to remain vigilant, avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, and familiarize themselves with emergency procedures.
Travelers were advised to identify nearby bomb shelters and download the Home Front Command's Red Alert application, or similar services, to receive real-time warnings about incoming rockets, missiles and armed drones.
Israel's Home Front Command emergency warning systems have been used during previous missile attacks, providing residents with alerts intended to help them reach protected areas.
The military has also updated its advance-warning capabilities to give civilians more time to prepare for certain missile threats.
The State Department encouraged American travelers to enroll in its Smart Traveler Enrollment Program, which enables the US Embassy to distribute security updates and contact citizens or their emergency contacts during a crisis.
Americans were also urged to develop independent evacuation plans that do not rely on US government assistance, follow instructions from local security officials, and exercise particular caution near checkpoints and areas with a significant security presence.
The advisory further recommended purchasing comprehensive travel insurance that covers emergency medical treatment, evacuation assistance, and trip cancellations.
The warnings underscore the continued importance of civilian preparedness amid regional missile and drone threats, with Israeli authorities having previously reviewed the timing and operation of emergency alerts during periods of heightened tensions.
Although the October 23 notice highlighted the increased potential for Houthi aggression, it did not announce additional restrictions on travel to Israel or a change in the State Department's assessment of the country's overall travel risk.

articles.title: Starlink in Ukraine Back to Normal After Week of Throttling
articles.body:
Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the U.S.
Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned systems came after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kilometers per hour (kph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
"The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the Telegram app.
According to Zelensky, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph.
Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries.
But Starlink remains vital for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year.
Limitations order
The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive U.S. intelligence.
Neither Musk nor the U.S. government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, U.S. administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.
On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "get it straightened out."
