articles.title: The limits of American power: Trump’s reckless gamble against Iran
articles.body:
The limits of American power: Trump’s reckless gamble against Iran
TEHRAN - The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has exposed the limits of American military power and the dangers of an administration that appears to have mistaken technological superiority for the ability to dictate political outcomes, William H. McRaven, who served in the U.S. Navy, wrote in Foreign Affairs.
Launched on February 28 without a clearly defined rationale or attainable objectives, the war illustrates Washington’s persistent failure to learn from the costly experiences of Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq.
From the outset, the Trump administration’s objectives have been inconsistent. Initially, Washington spoke of regime change and eliminating Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Later, reopening the Strait of Hormuz became a central priority, even though the waterway had not been closed before the war began. Trump’s contradictory statements about these objectives have raised serious questions about whether his administration had a coherent strategy or adequately considered the consequences of military action.
“The war was launched without a clear rationale and with a constantly shifting set of objectives—from changing Tehran’s regime and squelching its nuclear ambitions to, more recently, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which wasn’t closed until the war started. The results, not surprisingly, have been bad both for U.S. interests and for the Middle East,” McRaven stated.
At the heart of this failure lies an enduring American illusion: that overwhelming military superiority can overcome political, geographical, and strategic realities. Advanced aircraft, precision weapons, and sophisticated intelligence systems can inflict enormous damage, but they cannot automatically force a determined adversary to surrender or produce the political changes Washington desires. Iran’s geography, its capacity to challenge shipping through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, and its determination to resist foreign aggression all place significant limits on the effectiveness of American military power.
The administration’s approach has also undermined its international standing. According to the analysis, Washington launched the war without first building international legitimacy or consulting its allies, including neighboring Arab states. Its failure to acknowledge responsibility for an airstrike that reportedly killed 120 students at an Iranian elementary school further damaged its moral credibility. When Trump subsequently sought international assistance to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the administration encountered resistance from countries whose support it had failed to cultivate.
Such miscalculations reflect a broader problem in American policymaking: the growing concentration of presidential power and the politicization of institutions responsible for providing independent military, diplomatic, and intelligence advice. When personal loyalty takes precedence over professional judgment, warnings about the costs and risks of war may be ignored. The result can be a dangerous cycle in which overconfidence produces reckless decisions, and those decisions generate consequences that military force alone cannot reverse.
The experiences of Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq should have taught Washington that wars without clear objectives, broad international support, and realistic exit strategies can become prolonged strategic failures. Yet the Trump administration appears to have repeated these mistakes, underestimating both Iran’s capacity to resist and the broader regional consequences of attacking it.
Ultimately, the war underscores a fundamental truth: military supremacy does not amount to unlimited political power. Geography, national resistance, international legitimacy, and the quality of leadership remain decisive factors in determining the outcome of conflicts. The central lesson is clear: no amount of firepower can compensate for a reckless strategy, contradictory objectives, and a failure to understand the adversary.

articles.title: American are done paying for Trump’s family business
articles.body:
American are done paying for Trump’s family business
TEHRAN — Donald Trump won the White House promising to “Make America Great Again,” then promised Americans a short, cheap war on Iran. They got a closed Strait of Hormuz, Brent crude above $116 a barrel, and gasoline past $5 a gallon in several states. He and his family got a windfall.
Nine days before the November 3 midterms, the distance between those two experiences has become the central fact of American politics.
In CNBC’s final pre-election survey, 36 percent of registered voters named government corruption among their top issues, ahead of food prices at 34 percent and gasoline at 23 percent.
Fox News found 60 percent of voters extremely concerned. People are reading their grocery receipts and the headlines as one story.
A war with a customer list
The campaign of aggression against Iran has already cost tens of billions of dollars, paid from the public purse. Some of it is landing with companies the president’s sons own or advise.
Powerus, which Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are backing toward a stock listing, holds an Air Force contract worth up to $90 million for interceptors meant to counter Iranian drones.
Skeptics doubt the systems can stop Iran’s one-way attack drones, which have proved themselves in large numbers. Powerus is pitching them to Arab governments in the Persian Gulf anyway, the same clients Washington claims to be defending.
Trump Jr. also holds roughly $4 million in Unusual Machines, where he serves as an adviser. The “War” Department bought 3,500 drone motors and related parts from the company, and the Army has floated a follow-on order of 20,000.
Its shares jumped when his link became public. Rep. Jason Crow says firms tied to the sons have drawn about $3.7 billion in federal money this term.
The youngest Trump son, Barron, joined 1789 Capital days after the 2024 election. Among its holdings is Anduril, approved for a possible $2 billion interceptor sale to Kuwait.
Trump’s own portfolio includes Palantir, Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics and Northrop Grumman, whose revenues have swelled with U.S. military warmongering.
Richard Painter, who served as ethics lawyer in George W. Bush’s White House, told the Wall Street Journal that he sees no modern precedent. That is a notable benchmark, given the Bush administration’s own notorious record of foreign aggression and corporate enrichment.
Persian Gulf states, he says, are “under immense pressure to buy from Trump’s sons,” so the president will deliver what they want. It may be the first time, he adds, that a president’s family has made vast sums from a war launched without congressional authorization.
Arab monarchy money and a crypto pipeline
The Persian Gulf runs through the family’s earlier business too. In his upcoming book Princes and Thieves, Matthew Cole reports that Jared Kushner had access to at least two accounts tied to the UAE and Israel, together receiving about $2 billion, part of it Saudi-backed and moved through banks in Baku.
Dutch intelligence, which had penetrated his phone, helped trace the transfers. A third account, the report says, paid for an Israeli pledge to defend the Emirates against Iranian strikes.
Then came crypto. Days before the 2025 inauguration, an entity backed by Tahnoon bin Zayed, the UAE’s national security adviser, agreed to buy 49 percent of World Liberty Financial for $500 million.
An Abu Dhabi fund he chairs later bought $2 billion of the firm’s USD1 stablecoin. Months on, the administration eased AI chip exports to Emirati firms, including G42, which Tahnoon controls.
Trump also pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, whose company had paid $4.3 billion in fines, and accepted a $400 million jet from Qatar.
On October 22, a Circle shareholder sued in federal court, alleging violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause.
Trump’s disclosures show $2.2 billion in earnings for his first year back, $1.4 billion of it from crypto, including about $636 million from a memecoin whose promoters advertised a dinner with him for its 185 biggest holders.
‘Slime, not crime’
Smaller scandals keep piling up. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned after the Wall Street Journal reported she asked a donor to cover a $100,000 credit card bill.
Adviser Corey Lewandowski faces a Justice Department inquiry. The New York Times says Alina Habba, Trump’s former lawyer, agreed to a $50 million deal with the family of a Venezuelan billionaire who later received a pardon.
Trump’s answer was to warn that dishonest allies “have to be prosecuted,” while his Justice Department charged a Virginia Democrat, state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Expect few convictions. Experts point to the Supreme Court: McDonnell in 2016 narrowed “official acts,” Snyder in 2024 excused gratuities paid after the fact, and Trump v. United States granted presidents sweeping immunity.
The Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section was effectively shut down in February 2025. What remains, some prosecutors say, is “slime, not crime,” despite overwhelming evidence of corruption that Americans across party lines can no longer ignore.
Nine days to judgment
Voters have noticed anyway. A Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll found nearly two in three Americans think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, with most of the rise coming from Republicans and their leaners.
His approval sits at a record low of 33 percent, and Democrats have spent $182 million on corruption ads, more than the last four cycles combined, according to data from the firm AdImpact.
Vice President JD Vance calls the charge “laughable.” Trump’s pollster argues undecided voters will still choose on pocketbook issues. Perhaps. But $5 gasoline and a president’s sons selling drones are hard to pull apart.
The deeper question is what the money buys. In Matthew Cole’s account, Kushner held signing rights on an Emirati account while Abu Dhabi wanted the 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) dead.
Trump quit the agreement in May 2018. Months after he left office, Saudi Arabia’s sovereign fund gave his firm $2 billion, despite a screening panel finding its due diligence “unsatisfactory in all aspects.”
Today, at least some of the transactions happen in plain sight: Emirati stablecoin purchases, chip exports, drone contracts, and more.

articles.title: CIA contractor accused of leaking US reports on Israel to journalist girlfriend who published them
articles.body:
A classified U.S. intelligence assessment warning that Israel could descend into civil conflict, claims that Israeli officials pressed the Trump administration to assassinate a senior Iranian leader, and a secret report detailing efforts to secure American military support beyond Donald Trump's presidency are among the revelations at the center of a major intelligence leak scandal in Washington. 
On Friday, the FBI arrested a CIA contractor suspected of passing classified information to his journalist girlfriend, whose reporting included five stories based on sensitive intelligence, three of them directly concerning Israel.
The suspect, Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of Washington, D.C., held a Top Secret security clearance with access to highly sensitive intelligence. Prosecutors allege that for months he exploited his access to U.S. intelligence systems to examine classified reports unrelated to his duties and pass information to his romantic partner, who operated an independent news publication on Substack. Investigators linked his access to sensitive documents with telephone conversations between the couple and the publication dates of articles allegedly containing information from those reports.
American authorities have not publicly identified the journalist, referred to in the FBI affidavit as "Individual 1," or disclosed the subjects of the classified reports. However, documents obtained by ynet indicate that she is American journalist Aída Chávez, founder of the independent investigative publication Capital & Empire. Chávez previously worked for The Hill, contributed to The Washington Post and served as a congressional correspondent for The Intercept and Washington correspondent for The Nation. Five articles published on her website match the dates identified in the FBI affidavit, while a passage from a September fundraising appeal appears almost word for word in the document. Chávez has not been charged with any offense in connection with the investigation.
Israel's alleged assassination request and fears of civil war
One of the most significant articles appeared on May 28, under the headline "EXCLUSIVE: Israel Privately Pressing U.S. to Kill Iran's Lead Negotiator and Launch New Strikes." Chávez reported that Israeli officials had urged the Trump administration to assassinate Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran's parliament and a central figure in negotiations between Tehran and Washington. According to the report, Israel sought to persuade the Americans to abandon negotiations and resume attacks on Iran's oil infrastructure, believing further economic damage could trigger widespread protests and potentially bring down the Iranian regime.
Chávez said her reporting drew on a classified intelligence assessment circulated within the U.S. intelligence community and conversations with officials familiar with its contents. The FBI affidavit states that Brinksman accessed a classified report on May 26 and called his girlfriend three times that day. Two days later, she published an article that investigators say contained information from the same report.
Another article, published on July 29, described a U.S. intelligence assessment concerning Israel's efforts to preserve its strategic relationship with Washington as American public support for Israel weakened. According to Chávez, Israeli officials were seeking to embed their country more deeply within the American military, intelligence and defense industries, making it more difficult for future administrations to reduce cooperation. The reported strategy included discussions about a possible permanent U.S. military base in Israel, expanded joint weapons development and stronger ties with influential American technology executives. Investigators said Brinksman accessed a Top Secret document on July 28, spoke with his girlfriend several times that day and that an article containing information from the document appeared the following day.
The third Israel-related article, published on October 5 in cooperation with Drop Site News, concerned a reported CIA assessment titled "Fracture From Within." According to two American sources cited in the article, the assessment was prepared in August by the CIA's Red Cell, a unit tasked with challenging conventional intelligence assumptions and examining alternative scenarios. It warned that Israel's political crisis, disputes over military conscription for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, economic pressure, social divisions and the psychological consequences of prolonged warfare could combine to produce severe internal conflict or even institutional breakdown ahead of the October 27 election.
The reported assessment raised concerns about armed military veterans returning from combat with psychological trauma, worsening political polarization and mounting resentment over exemptions from military service. It also examined the possibility of foreign technology companies withdrawing from Israel, deteriorating regional relationships and Hamas or Hezbollah exploiting domestic instability. Crucially, the report did not constitute an official U.S. intelligence prediction that civil war would occur. It was an assessment of potential risks and scenarios, as described by the journalist's sources.
The FBI affidavit details another striking sequence of events. Brinksman allegedly accessed a classified document several times in August and again on October 1. Telephone records show that he spoke with his girlfriend for 47 minutes that day, followed by another conversation lasting 37 minutes. Four days later, the article on Israel's potential internal collapse appeared.
The two remaining articles concerned other Middle Eastern developments. On March 11, Chávez reported that Bahrain had brought in forces from Jordan to help suppress protests over its involvement in the war with Iran. On May 13, she reported on a classified CIA assessment describing divisions among Washington's Gulf allies, with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain favoring continued strikes against Iran while Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait preferred renewed negotiations. Investigators allege that classified information accessed by Brinksman also appeared in these reports.
More than 800 calls and a trail of classified documents
The evidence that led investigators to Brinksman is detailed in a 13-page FBI affidavit. He began working for a U.S. government agency in 2020 before moving to a contractor serving the same agency. In 2022, he took a position involving computer systems integration, including work transferring data between classified and unclassified systems. CIA Director John Ratcliffe confirmed that Brinksman had provided services to the agency.
His position required him to work inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF, a secure area where personal phones and electronic devices are prohibited. Employees must use identification cards to enter and leave, creating records that became central to the investigation. According to the FBI, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified reports, left the secure area and contacted his girlfriend, sometimes within minutes. Investigators believe these intervals allowed him to retrieve his personal phone, possibly from his vehicle, and communicate sensitive information.
In one example, the journalist called Brinksman at 8:41 a.m. on March 11. Less than half an hour later, he accessed a classified intelligence report at 9:09 a.m. and again at 10:01 a.m. He subsequently left the secure facility and received another call from her that evening, lasting about 14 minutes. An article published that day allegedly contained Top Secret information from the document he had examined.
Investigators found records of more than 800 telephone calls or attempted calls between the couple during 2026. They also examined computers at Brinksman's workplace and discovered that he was among no more than six people who had accessed the journalist's Substack publication from that facility during the period under investigation. According to the affidavit, no other individual combined access to all five classified reports with visits to all five articles that authorities believe contained information from those documents.
A notebook discovered on Brinksman's desk on October 10 also attracted investigators' attention because corners had been torn from several pages. An FBI agent noted that individuals who transmit sensitive information sometimes write notes to reproduce accurate or near-verbatim quotations. However, the affidavit did not establish that the notebook contained leaked secrets or provide direct evidence that its missing pages had been used to transmit information.
‘I'm helping her build her publication’
One of the most personal details in the investigation emerged from an email Brinksman sent to a friend in November 2025. He described his new relationship with a journalist who had recently become independent and explained that he was helping her establish a publication focused on foreign policy. He added that the project had proved surprisingly fulfilling. Other emails examined by investigators supported the conclusion that the two were romantically involved.
According to the affidavit, their collaboration extended beyond conversations about published stories. On March 13, Brinksman received permission to edit a Google Docs document concerning a Middle Eastern country. Minutes later, he suggested a wording change, which his girlfriend marked as resolved. The article published that day matches a Chávez report concerning Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer, a prominent supporter of Israel, and congressional votes related to the war with Iran. Investigators did not identify classified information in that particular article. Brinksman had also sought advance publication clearance, as required of security clearance holders, for articles he co-authored with the journalist.
Brinksman's background adds an unusual dimension to the allegations. A graduate of Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service, he co-authored a study published in May 2019 titled "Millennial Considerations on Insider Threat: Are We A Threat Or An Opportunity?" The research examined the risks posed by employees with access to sensitive information and proposed measures to prevent security breaches, including employee training, monitoring potential warning signs and addressing vulnerabilities associated with social media and mobile technology. Seven years later, Brinksman faces allegations involving precisely the kind of insider threat his research sought to help organizations prevent.
Chávez describes Capital & Empire as an independent publication investigating the interests driving American military and economic policy. In a September fundraising appeal, she said she had published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that she believed the public deserved to know about. She also encouraged readers with inside information to provide leaks.
Brinksman has been charged with unlawfully transmitting national defense information, an offense carrying a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg accused him of going far beyond his duties to obtain closely guarded American intelligence and passing it to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish it. Eisenberg described the alleged conduct as a betrayal of the trust placed in someone holding a security clearance. FBI Director Kash Patel pledged to pursue anyone who abuses access to government secrets, while Ratcliffe said the arrest followed a referral from the CIA and warned that unauthorized disclosures could endanger intelligence sources, ongoing operations and agency personnel. Brinksman remains presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

articles.title: Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
The United States appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran, but there is unlikely to be a military solution for either side in the devastating conflict, experts say.
Washington and Tehran's forces have settled into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships, with the United States seeking to enforce a blockade of Iran's ports and the Islamic republic trying to exert control over the key Strait of Hormuz waterway.
Neither country has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, but that may soon change.
"I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to November 3 elections in the United States.
She pointed to potential signs including the movement of additional US military assets and troops to the Middle East, warnings issued to Americans in the region, and a high alert status for Israeli forces.
Additionally, President Donald Trump "came out publicly and said that he wouldn't strike before the midterms," and "it wouldn't seem to help him at the polls to do so," Maloney said.
The US-Israeli war against Iran -- launched in late February -- is largely unpopular in the United States, especially because it has sharply driven up fuel prices, and is likely to be a drag on Trump's Republican Party in the key vote.
"Fundamentally, the situation isn't sustainable in its current state," Maloney said, noting that the US blockade is "creating greater pain for the Iranians," while Washington has a large number of naval assets tied up in enforcing it.
"There has to be some kind of a resolution, either through diplomacy or through military action," she said.
Asked about the Iran on Friday, Trump told journalists that "we could end it very quickly," but said the question is "do we want to finish it off, or... do we just want to let it wither?"
Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, meanwhile said Friday that there could "absolutely" be a strike this weekend, ahead of Tuesday's Israeli elections.
'Impossible to predict'
Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said there have "certainly been recent signs that renewed strikes may be in the offing," or that "the US is expecting strikes carried out by Iran" or their Houthi allies in Yemen.
He noted the planned deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East -- which could at least temporarily bring the number of carrier strike groups there to three -- as well as the decision to dispatch another Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region.
Campbell also said Israeli warplanes recently carried out a "show of force" mimicking previous strikes on Iran, and noted that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.
However, "timing here is impossible to predict," he said of renewed strikes, while noting that "this is admittedly an expansive set of actions to take if the intent is to simply pressure Iran to the negotiating table."
Campbell said Trump's options are more limited than they were earlier in the conflict, with damage to US bases in the region having made any potential ground operation more difficult.
"At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands (in some scenarios tens of thousands) of forces that would be required for such an operation," he said.
Maloney meanwhile said that "most of the conventional military sites (in Iran) have already been heavily degraded" by previous strikes, meaning any new campaign will likely "entail more strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets that impact the Iranian population."
But that -- or any type of military action -- is unlikely to bring about a resolution to the conflict.
"From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said.
Campbell agreed, saying: "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime."
"They have demonstrated a willingness to absorb a significant amount of physical pain and even some alterations to targeting that includes key mixed or even civilian infrastructure will not significantly change this," he added.

articles.title: Israeli-born oligarch behind Russia's $14 billion sanctions-evading cash network linked to Iran, Hamas
articles.body:
As Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu calls for Israel to prepare an economy capable of operating around international sanctions, one Israeli citizen has already become a central figure in Russia's efforts to circumvent Western financial restrictions. Ilan Shor, a Moldovan oligarch born in Israel who holds Israeli citizenship, is behind a vast Russian payment network that has processed billions of dollars since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. American authorities now accuse that network of serving not only Russia but also Iran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Hamas. 
Four and a half years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin has developed an array of mechanisms to keep international trade and financial transactions moving despite Western sanctions. One of the most significant is A7, an international payments company established in 2024 by Shor, 39. He holds a 51% stake in the company, while the remaining 49% belongs to Promsvyazbank, or PSB, a Russian state-owned bank itself subject to extensive international sanctions.
An investigation published this week by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), working with independent Russian media outlet Proekt, revealed the extraordinary scale of A7's operations. Between November 2024 and July 2025, the company processed at least 283 tons of Russian banknotes, worth more than $14 billion. Internal documents showed how the company used cash brokers, financial intermediaries and companies registered outside Russia to help businesses complete payments that conventional banking channels had made increasingly difficult. 
How billions in Russian cash reach foreign suppliers
At the heart of the operation is Moscow's Sadovod Market, a sprawling wholesale and retail complex in the southeastern part of the Russian capital. According to the investigation, brokers operating there receive payment instructions from Russian businesses seeking to purchase goods overseas, particularly from Chinese suppliers. Rather than transferring money directly through Russian banks, clients hand over large quantities of rubles in cash.
The brokers place the banknotes in numbered bags, which are transported to an A7 cash-processing center. There, teams of cashiers count the money and record the amounts, bag numbers and payment instructions. The cash is then delivered to PSB, which deposits the funds into A7 accounts. Companies registered outside Russia subsequently arrange payments to foreign recipients, often through intermediaries in Kyrgyzstan, Hong Kong and other jurisdictions. The result, investigators found, is that the Chinese banks receiving the transfers may have no visibility into the original Russian source of the money.
The scale of the transactions is substantial. A payment register from late 2024 contained approximately 2,300 proposed or documented transfers linked to brokers at Sadovod, most intended for recipients in mainland China or Hong Kong. Many were routed through accounts belonging to a Kyrgyz state-owned trading company. A7 has also promoted the speed of its system, announcing in December 2025 that it had completed a transfer to China in just one hour and 40 minutes. 
The Kremlin has taken a direct interest in the project. During a video conference with President Vladimir Putin in September 2025, Shor presented A7's achievements and plans for expansion. He reported that the platform was processing approximately 1,500 to 2,000 transactions daily and described payment volumes running into trillions of rubles. The company also outlined plans to expand its operations in Asia, where it said more than half of its payments were being directed. These figures were company claims and have not all been independently verified.
US sanctions and alleged connections to Iran and Hamas
On October 1, the U.S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions on the A7 network, designating it a significant transnational criminal organization. The department described A7 as a shadow banking operation that uses money-laundering techniques to disguise illicit payments as legitimate commercial transactions and move enormous sums across borders in violation of sanctions and other laws.
The American allegations extend far beyond Russian trade. According to the Treasury Department, A7 has provided financial support to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Iranian-backed organizations, including Hamas. U.S. authorities also linked the network to Nobitex, Iran's largest digital asset exchange, sanctioned by Washington in June 2026, and to transactions associated with North Korean cryptocurrency exchange hacks and other illicit activity.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the action was intended to dismantle financial infrastructure that enables Iran and other U.S. adversaries to evade sanctions and move illicit funds. A7 has rejected the American allegations of wrongdoing, saying it operates compliance procedures and was established to facilitate payments for Russian businesses facing what it considers illegitimate restrictions. The company's denials include the allegations concerning Iran and terrorist organizations. 
From Israel to the Kremlin's protection
Shor's personal history is as unusual as the financial operation he now oversees. Born in Tel Aviv in 1987 to a family originally from Moldova, he moved with his parents to Chisinau during the 1990s. His father, Miron Shor, established a successful duty-free retail business, which Ilan joined as a young man. After his father's death, he took control of the family enterprise and expanded into other sectors, building a business empire before entering Moldovan politics.
His political career was overshadowed by one of Moldova's largest financial scandals. In 2017, Shor was convicted in connection with the theft of approximately $1 billion from the country's banking system, a case widely known in Moldova as the "theft of the century." Initially sentenced to seven and a half years in prison, he remained free during his appeal and fled to Israel in 2019. In April 2023, a Moldovan appeals court increased his prison sentence to 15 years for fraud and money laundering. His political party was subsequently banned. Shor has maintained that he was the victim of political persecution by Moldova's pro-Western authorities. 
After spending several years in Israel, Shor relocated to Russia, where he emerged as an outspoken supporter of Putin and increasingly appeared in Kremlin-aligned media. Despite remaining wanted by Moldova, he has continued to conduct major business operations from Russia under the protection of the country's political establishment. His role in A7 has made him a prominent figure in Moscow's efforts to maintain international financial connections despite Western restrictions.
The revelations come as Netanyahu warns that Israel could eventually face economic and banking sanctions of its own and has instructed advisers to examine alternative financial arrangements, including blockchain technology and cryptocurrencies. Netanyahu has not proposed adopting A7's methods, and his comments concerned preparations for possible future restrictions, rather than sanctions already imposed on Israel's banking system. Nevertheless, Shor's story illustrates both the scale that sanctions-resistant payment networks can reach and the serious legal and security consequences they can face when their activities attract international scrutiny.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthi missile shrapnel falls in Jeddah, Taif, Rabigh after interceptions
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said on Saturday it intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by Yemen's Houthis toward the Mecca and Medina regions, with debris falling in several locations, including Jeddah, Taif, and Rabigh.
This follows a Houthi announcement about attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, including a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
The terror group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said it also targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, as well as Najran airport and an air base in Khamis Mushait.
Houthi media reports strikes on Sanaa
Earlier on Saturday, Houthi-linked Saba News Agency reported that Yemen’s National Commission for Human Rights had condemned Saudi Arabia over strikes in the capital.
The group described a “massacre” in the Asr neighborhood of Sanaa and an attack on a cement factory in the Hamdan district of Sanaa Governorate.
US warns Americans about possible escalation in Middle East
The latest round of strikes came amid warnings by the US State Department, which updated its travel advisory notice for Israel on Friday, warning of an increased threat of armed attacks by Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and the potential for a rapid escalation of regional hostilities.
The update did not change Israel's overall travel advisory classification, which remains at Level 3, urging American citizens to reconsider travel due to terrorism and unrest. The existing risk indicators and restrictions on travel to certain areas of the country also remain unchanged.
In its warning on armed conflict, the State Department cited previous Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure that resulted in civilian casualties and major travel disruptions.
Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

articles.title: Israel brings talks with Lebanon to a standstill by refusing to withdraw from ‘pilot zones’
articles.body:
Israel brings talks with Lebanon to a standstill by refusing to withdraw from ‘pilot zones’
Talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials, hosted by the US in Tampa, Florida, this week, concluded without any breakthroughs, The New Arab reported on Thursday, citing its own sources.
The discussions were held at US Central Command headquarters, the Pentagon's Middle East operations arm. They come as Israel has continued its attacks on Lebanon this month, carrying out air strikes and home demolitions in the Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil, and Sidon districts.
The New Arab said it was told there was "intransigence in Israeli positions, while the Lebanese side is holding firm to its demands that steps must be reciprocal".
The Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF), largely funded by the US, has also rejected direct military-to-military coordination with the Israelis, instead preferring a third-party verification mechanism to be employed by the United Nations and allies such as France.
Israel has bombed Lebanon consistently since October 2023, after the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel ignited the region.
A November 2024 ceasefire brokered by the former Biden administration did little to curb Israel's insistence that it was targeting Hezbollah leaders and weapons depots across the country, including in the capital, Beirut.
But it wasn't until this year that Israel significantly ramped up its military operations, mounted a ground invasion, and occupied long stretches of the south and east of Lebanon.
Since the US and Israel launched their joint war on Iran on 28 February, which prompted Hezbollah to launch attacks on Israel in defense of its ally, Israel has killed more than 4,300 Lebanese and displaced one million people in the country.
Lebanese officials have prioritized returning the displaced to their lands and demanded a timetable to do so from the Israelis, but there has been no movement on the issue since the US-sponsored framework was signed by the two sides in June.
Lebanon and Israel agreed to a trilateral framework with the Trump administration in Washington earlier this year, following five rounds of talks hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The three countries held what was billed as a historic signing ceremony on 26 June.
Rubio said it was "the beginning of the beginning" in remarks to reporters at the time.
He later added the US would commit $100m in "humanitarian assistance in coordination with the UN" for affected communities, though he did not specify whether it was just for Lebanon or also for northern Israeli border towns.
Rubio said the LAF would be "reimbursed" by the Trump administration to the tune of $30m.
The framework led to the creation of the Military Coordination Group for Lebanon, which Washington would facilitate.
But the "pilot zones" that the Israelis pledged to withdraw from, in order to allow the LAF to take over, have not been expanded since July, with the Israelis claiming that the LAF have not had the capacity to disarm Hezbollah fighters.
Hezbollah is the key party to the conflict that was not represented in the talks.
It remains the country's most powerful military organization and far outmatches the LAF's capabilities. It was formed in the 1980s in response to the illegal Israeli occupation of Lebanon.
It has insisted that it cannot disarm while Israel remains a threat to Lebanon, and as Israeli officials normalize rhetoric about expanding Israel's borders to the north.

articles.title: Iran's president calls for renewed US talks; Report: Hezbollah vows to stay out of another war
articles.body:
Hezbollah has informed Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri that it does not intend to intervene on Iran's behalf if a new war breaks out between Tehran and the United States and Israel, Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat reported Saturday. The reported assurance comes amid growing fears of renewed military confrontation and warnings that another conflict could have devastating consequences for Lebanon.
According to Lebanese parliamentary sources cited by the newspaper, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh told lawmakers affiliated with Hezbollah and the allied Amal Movement during a recent visit to Beirut that Tehran would not ask the Lebanese terrorist group to participate in another war. Iran, he reportedly said, was capable of defending itself against American attacks without Hezbollah's assistance.
"We have made significant progress in our preparations to prevent the United States from achieving its objectives," Khatibzadeh reportedly told the lawmakers. The sources said Tehran's position reflected the significant military imbalance between Hezbollah and Israel, which meant that Hezbollah's involvement would be unlikely to alter the outcome of a broader confrontation.
Another consideration is the potential backlash from Hezbollah's own supporters. According to the report, Lebanon's Shiite community would be unlikely to accept another costly war fought on Iran's behalf, particularly after the heavy losses and displacement caused by previous confrontations with Israel. Hezbollah's leadership would face considerable difficulty justifying another intervention.
However, the Iranian Embassy in Lebanon issued a statement Saturday denying media reports concerning Khatibzadeh's recent visit and the contents of his meetings, casting doubt on the account attributed to the Iranian official.
Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian appeared to favor renewed diplomacy. Speaking on Iranian state television Saturday, he blamed Washington for the collapse of an earlier agreement but said negotiations should resume. "We were having negotiations. The cowards ruined everything. I still think we should complete it," he said.
Diplomatic contacts have continued despite the escalating rhetoric. Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, who has played a mediating role between Washington and Tehran since their most recent ceasefire, visited Iran earlier this week. A Qatar-based media report subsequently claimed that the two sides had reached preliminary understandings on resuming negotiations, including measures to prevent renewed fighting and the possible release of $6 billion in Iranian funds held in Qatari banks.
Yet Iranian officials offered a far more pessimistic assessment in comments to Reuters, saying Tehran expected the United States and Israel to resume military operations rather than reach an agreement. One official said Iran was preparing for renewed attacks, while others acknowledged that Tehran had deliberately prolonged negotiations in hopes of weakening President Donald Trump politically ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections.
The growing tensions have also prompted Washington to reduce its diplomatic presence across the Middle East. According to an intelligence memorandum dated October 23 and reported by Axios, Iran has significantly intensified efforts to target American diplomats and senior officials abroad, with alleged assassination plots reaching advanced stages. The warning has contributed to heightened security measures at U.S. diplomatic missions.
Trump added to the uncertainty Friday during a rally in Florida, warning that another American military operation against Iran remained possible unless Tehran agreed to a deal. "We may do another little Operation Epic Fury, or the Iranians will agree to a deal," he said, adding that Iran should return to negotiations.
With Iranian missile testing reportedly continuing and Washington preparing for the possibility of renewed hostilities, Hezbollah's reported decision to remain on the sidelines could prove significant. Whether the group would maintain that position if fighting resumed, however, remains uncertain.

articles.title: Air Force Considering Air-to-Air Role for Bombers amid Fighter Procurement Constraints
articles.body:
The Air Force’s future strategy for fighting wars could include arming bombers with air-to-air strike capabilities, the service said in a new report to Congress.
The report, titled “Long-Term USAF Fighter Force Structure” and submitted to lawmakers Oct. 16, said that “developing air-to-air capabilities on bombers” is being considered as a way to expand the service’s combat capabilities.
In the report, which was briefed to reporters Oct. 20 and obtained by Air & Space Forces Magazine, the Air Force estimates it will need 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035 to meet the demands of the National Defense Strategy at moderate risk, with about 40 percent of its fighter fleet consisting of F-35A Joint Strike Fighters. That’s up from the 1,288 combat-coded fighters the service has today.
The Air Force is working on ways to procure as many Lockheed Martin F-35As, Boeing F-15EX Eagle IIs, and Boeing F-47 sixth-generation fighters as possible, the report said. However, the report acknowledges that hitting its fighter procurement targets may not be achievable due to “fiscal realities and industrial production limitations.”
Other recapitalization options could include acquiring an entirely new fighter, relying more on semi-autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft—and giving air-to-air roles and capabilities to bombers, the report said.
Air Force fighters have long carried out air-to-ground strikes, but bombers have not traditionally performed air-to-air missions.
However, with the Air Force’s fleet constrained by slow procurement of new fighters and the retirement of aging ones, the service has been looking for new ways to accomplish its missions.
Former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin signaled an openness to the B-21 Raider stealth bomber carrying out a greater role in the service’s air dominance plans in an October 2024 discussion with reporters in Washington.
At the time, the Air Force had put its F-47 program—then called Next-Generation Air Dominance—on hold amid concerns about its potential costs. The Air Force was reviewing its approach to air superiority to try to figure out ways to get the job done, potentially without the plane that would become the F-47.
When asked if the air superiority review could lead to a more prominent role for the B-21, Allvin said “We have not taken that off the table.”
A year later, in September 2025, sources told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the Air Force was studying whether a large flying wing-type stealth aircraft—potentially based on a B-21—armed with dozens of air-to-air missiles could be an element of its future air superiority force.
In its latest report, the Air Force wrote that it is “committed to the full modernization and recapitalization of its legacy fighter fleet, while placing an enormous effort into our newest fighter, the F-47.”
CCAs are also rapidly advancing and likely to at least meet, if not beat, the program’s schedule, the report said. But the Air Force said CCAs aren’t yet ready to change how the service plans for its future fighter fleet, though that day will come.
“There is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters,” Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, told reporters Oct. 20.
The report also said it will be “essential” to modernize its current cadre of older F-15s and F-16s into a fleet of “advanced fourth-generation capability” jets—planes that do not have stealth capabilities but can still operate in highly contested environments, often with the aid of advanced sensors and electronic warfare weapons.
But it would take more than a decade of investments in the Air Force’s current depot infrastructure to modernize enough jets to increase the Air Force’s aircraft availability, the report said, calling that approach “insufficient, as it perpetuates reliance on a fleet averaging 30+ years in age.”
Aside from upgrading existing fighters, the service could also buy new advanced fourth-gen jets like the F-15EX and, potentially, a new version of Lockheed Martin’s F-16 Fighting Falcon, dubbed the F-16G. Tabor said the service has not yet made any decision on buying new F-16s, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.”
In its report, the Air Force said it has to pursue a two-track strategy of modernizing existing aircraft to meet immediate operational requirements, while recapitalizing its legacy fighters at the same time.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force details $20.7B AMRAAM missile contract
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon a $20.7 billion sole-source contract for AMRAAM Production Lots 41 through 47, with work in Tucson through June 2033.
- A 2017 justification document found no other company interested in becoming a second source for AMRAAM production.
The U.S. Air Force has published new details of its $20.7 billion contract with Raytheon for AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, confirming that the sole-source deal covers seven production lots and will keep the Tucson, Arizona, production line busy until mid-2033.
An award notice posted on the federal contracting site on Oct. 23, 2026, shows the fixed-price incentive contract was signed on Sept. 25 for AMRAAM Production Lots 41 through 47. It covers AMRAAM missiles, AMRAAM telemetry sets used in testing, initial and field spares and other production components, with all work in Tucson and an expected completion date of June 30, 2033. The notice gives a base and all options value of $20,699,334,581 but does not list how many missiles the contract buys.
RTX announced the deal on Sept. 28 as a multiyear contract worth up to $20.7 billion over five years, with two option years, for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and international customers buying through Foreign Military Sales. The award is more than five times the size of the previous record AMRAAM contract, a $3.5 billion award in July 2025 for Lots 39 and 40, which itself surpassed a $1.19 billion contract for Lot 38 in September 2024.
The AMRAAM is the primary beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile of the United States and many allies, guided by an active radar seeker with mid-course GPS guidance and a two-way datalink. Raytheon says it is fielded by 44 countries on 14 platforms, from fighters such as the F-15, F-16, F/A-18, F-22 and F-35 to the ground-based NASAMS air defense system widely used in Ukraine and across Europe. Recent lots have included the AIM-120D-3 for U.S. services and the AIM-120C-8 for export customers.
The Air Force awarded the contract without competition under federal acquisition rules that allow a sole-source buy when only one responsible source can meet the requirement. A justification notice tied to the award was published the same day, and an earlier class justification signed in 2018 for Lots 34 through 43 lays out the reasoning the service has used for years.
That document traces Raytheon’s position to 1997, when Raytheon and Hughes Missile Systems Company, which the government had funded as competing AMRAAM producers, merged into Raytheon Missile Systems and left a single contractor able to develop, produce and sustain the missile. The program office concluded that qualifying a second source would require buying the technical data package, replicating the factory and requalifying suppliers, at a cost that competition would not recover, and that suppliers below Raytheon would remain sole sources regardless.
“No company has expressed any desire to be a second source for AMRAAM production/sustainment,” the 2017 justification states.
A 2017 market survey drew only limited interest, all of it in managing obsolete parts rather than building missiles, and the interested parties either withdrew or said their services were better suited to a subcontracting role.
The new contract comes as the Department of War pushes to rebuild missile stocks. Under a February 2026 framework agreement, RTX committed to producing at least 1,900 AMRAAMs a year, and the company says it nearly doubled output in 2025 compared with 2024. Work on Lots 41 through 47 is scheduled to run through June 30, 2033.

articles.title: British ships defy Chinese warnings in South China Sea
articles.body:
Two Royal Navy patrol ships have finished a ten day exercise in the South China Sea alongside Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, working with fifth generation fighters, a Singaporean submarine and New Zealand boarding teams, according to the Royal Navy.
HMS Spey and HMS Tamar led the British contribution to Bersama Lima 2026, the annual exercise of the Five Power Defence Arrangements, whose name means Together Five in Malay. The participating navies brought corvettes, frigates, patrol ships and a submarine, and the exercise built from familiarisation scenarios to a two day war game.
Before sailing, the crews spent a week learning each other’s vessels, systems, procedures and the language they would use at sea so that they could work together once the pace picked up. The maritime phase covered boarding and searching suspect vessels, naval gunfire directed onto targets ashore by soldiers embarked in the ships, a submarine hunt and an air defence exercise supported by aircraft.
Commander Tom Lindsey, the commanding officer of HMS Tamar, said: “Bersama Lima was an excellent opportunity to put my ship’s company through their paces and refresh their war-fighting skills with our Five Power allies.
“There was a great breadth to this iteration of Bersama Lima: fifth-generation fighter jets, international boarding teams and Singapore’s newest submarine which, combined with the level of competence and professionalism showed, levelled up the experience gained.
“These war-fighting serials demonstrated that we can put a task group together in short order and successfully operate together to achieve a spectrum of scenarios.”
Tamar hosted a Royal New Zealand Navy Deployable Boarding Team which was put through repeated serials investigating suspected illegal fishing and narcotics smuggling, work the team and the ship will be doing for real on their next mission.
Able Seaman Mansfield, one of Tamar’s seaman specialists, said: “Driving a Kiwi boarding team up to a suspect vessel with a second sea boat, armed to the teeth, was a surreal experience which really brought the exercise to life.
“We also got the opportunity to replenish underway at sea where we exchanged some goods from home with HMAS Stalwart, who sent Tim Tams [Australia’s favourite biscuit] in return!”
A sailor from HMS Spey said: “It was a privilege to attend Bersama Lima 26 alongside our FPDA partners, an exercise which demonstrates over five decades of commitment to training and working together.
“Throughout the harbour phase, HMS Spey’s sailors took the opportunity to learn from each of the Five Power nations and share their skills to enhance interoperability and build stronger friendships in the region.”
Each British operation in the region since has drawn the same response as Beijing previously accused Britain of flexing its naval muscles over the 2021 carrier deployment. After HMS Spey passed through the Taiwan Strait in June 2025, Senior Captain Liu Runke, spokesman for the navy of the People’s Liberation Army Eastern Theatre Command, said British remarks about the transit had distorted legal principles, and that troops remained on high alert and would resolutely counter all threats and provocations.
When Spey exercised navigation rights and freedoms around the Spratly Islands in May this year, China’s ambassador to the United Kingdom said the 2016 arbitration award was illegal, null and void and that the British position would not shake China’s resolve, as this publication reported at the time. In July the Chinese Embassy in London told Britain to stop stirring up trouble after it backed a statement on the same award, and the embassy’s position was set out again as the two ships entered the sea at the start of this month.
Spey and Tamar are Batch 2 River class offshore patrol vessels, each crewed by around sixty sailors. They have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021 under Operation Highwall. The Five Power Defence Arrangements date from 1971 and remain the only standing multilateral defence arrangement in the region involving Britain.
Spey is now heading to south-east Asia for several weeks of patrols and diplomatic engagement, while Tamar is making for Australia and New Zealand by way of Pacific island chains, where she will carry out maritime security patrols and counter illegal fishing.

articles.title: General Staff: Ukraine strikes Tolyattikauchuk plant, missile component manufacturer and aircraft in Yeysk
articles.body:
General Staff: Ukraine strikes Tolyattikauchuk plant, missile component manufacturer and aircraft in Yeysk
Ukraine's defence forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk plant, Proton-Electrotex – a company which produces missile components – and an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in Russia on 23 October and on the night of 23-24 October.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Details: A strike on the main production building of Proton-Electrotex JSC in the city of Oryol has been confirmed.
According to the General Staff, the company produces, among other things, components for S-71 Kovyor cruise missiles and Iskander-M ballistic missiles and is involved in the production of Pantsir-S1 air defence missile and gun systems.
The Tolyattikauchuk plant in Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, was also struck. An explosion and fire were recorded in the vicinity of the facility.
The General Staff noted that the plant produces synthetic rubber and other products used, among other things, in the manufacture of solid rocket propellant.
In addition, an aircraft was struck at the Yeysk airfield in Russia's Krasnodar Krai. The extent of the damage is being assessed.
Background: The Russian-installed occupation authorities reported a blackout in Sevastopol and other cities in Crimea.

articles.title: The new Arab bargain: When Egypt offers to protect Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
When Egyptian officials signalled their readiness to support Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, the announcement was presented as a familiar display of Arab solidarity. Yet beneath the diplomatic rhetoric lies a much more significant story, one that says less about military cooperation and more about the changing balance of power in the Middle East.
The immediate question appears straightforward: What kind of protection can Egypt realistically offer Saudi Arabia?
The more important question is whether Egypt’s offer reveals that the traditional hierarchy of the Arab world has been quietly reversed.
For decades, Egypt occupied a unique position in Arab politics. It was the state that projected military weight, diplomatic influence, and cultural authority across the region. Saudi Arabia possessed financial power, but Cairo was widely regarded as the Arab world’s strategic center of gravity.
Today, however, the relationship between the two countries is increasingly defined by a different reality. Egypt remains demographically and militarily significant, but its economic fragility has created a level of dependence on Gulf stability that would have been almost unimaginable in previous generations.
The offer to help defend Saudi Arabia therefore deserves to be viewed not as a demonstration of Egyptian strength, but as evidence of a broader geopolitical transformation.
Military realities explain why.
Despite possessing one of the Arab world’s largest armed forces, Egypt is neither politically nor economically positioned to undertake a large-scale military intervention in Yemen.
The trauma of Gamal Abdel Nasser’s disastrous Yemen campaign in the 1960s remains deeply embedded in Egyptian strategic thinking. That conflict consumed enormous military resources, cost thousands of lives, and distracted Cairo from more immediate national priorities.
No Egyptian leadership is likely to repeat that experience.
Moreover, Egypt today faces a crowded security agenda closer to home. Instability in Sudan, uncertainty in Libya, tensions in the Red Sea, challenges in Sinai, and concerns surrounding the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam all compete for Cairo’s attention. Under such circumstances, the prospect of deploying large numbers of Egyptian troops into another protracted Yemeni conflict appears highly improbable.
If Egypt contributes militarily, its role will likely be concentrated in the maritime domain: securing sea lanes, protecting Red Sea navigation routes, enhancing intelligence cooperation, and supporting regional deterrence efforts. These are meaningful contributions, but they fall far short of the image invoked by traditional narratives of Arab military intervention.
This is where the deeper story emerges.
The Houthis are not merely threatening Saudi Arabia. They are threatening Egypt’s economic lifeline.
The disruption of shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait has severely affected traffic through the Suez Canal, one of Egypt’s most important sources of foreign currency. Every escalation in the Red Sea directly translates into economic pressure on Cairo.
In practical terms, Egypt’s interest in stabilizing the Gulf and confronting threats to regional navigation is not an act of altruism; it is an act of economic self-preservation.
That should not be surprising.
States do not mobilize because of gratitude. They mobilize because of interests.
Yet Middle Eastern political discourse still tends to frame relations between Arab states through the language of fraternity, loyalty, and historical obligation. Such language often obscures what is actually taking place. Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia is driven not by sentiment but by a recognition that Egyptian prosperity is increasingly linked to Gulf stability.
The irony is striking.
For much of the twentieth century, wealthy Arab states depended upon Egypt as a source of political legitimacy, military expertise, and strategic backing. Today, Egypt’s own economic stability has become intertwined with Gulf investment, Gulf aid, and Gulf confidence.
This is not a temporary fluctuation. It reflects a structural shift in how power operates within the Arab world.
The rise of Gulf sovereign wealth funds, ambitious development strategies, and expanding regional investment networks has altered the traditional equation. Political influence is no longer derived primarily from military manpower or ideological leadership. It increasingly flows from economic resilience, investment capacity, and the ability to shape regional outcomes through finance.
Under this new reality, Saudi Arabia has become not merely an oil producer or regional actor, but one of the principal anchors of economic stability across significant parts of the Arab world.
Seen from this perspective, another apparent contradiction suddenly becomes easier to understand.
While expressing support for Saudi Arabia, Egypt also maintains diplomatic communication with Iran. To some observers, this appears inconsistent. Why would Cairo coordinate with Riyadh while simultaneously engaging Tehran?
The answer lies in the changing nature of Middle Eastern politics.
The region no longer operates according to the rigid bloc politics that defined much of the past decade. Saudi Arabia itself has restored relations with Iran. The United Arab Emirates maintains extensive economic links with Tehran. Across the region, governments increasingly seek to combine deterrence with dialogue rather than choose between them.
Egypt’s communication with Iran therefore reflects a wider regional trend: reducing the risk of escalation while maintaining strategic alignments. Cairo has little interest in becoming a frontline participant in a broader regional confrontation. Its primary objective is stability, particularly in waterways and trade corridors that directly affect its economic survival.
This calculation exposes a larger truth about the contemporary Middle East.
The old question, “Who protects whom?” may no longer make sense.
Saudi Arabia does not require Egyptian divisions stationed on the Yemeni front to guarantee its security. Equally, Egypt cannot sustain its economic stability without a relatively secure Gulf environment. What has emerged instead is a relationship of mutual dependence, in which military capability and economic power reinforce one another.
The traditional image of Egypt as the Arab world’s protector and Saudi Arabia as its financier belongs increasingly to another era.
A new bargain is taking shape.
Egypt remains too important to be ignored. Saudi Arabia remains too influential to be separated from broader Arab stability. Yet neither country occupies the role it once held. The balance has become more symmetrical, more transactional, and arguably more honest.
That is why Egypt’s offer to defend Saudi Arabia matters.
Not because it signals the beginning of a new war, but because it reveals the emergence of a new Arab order. An order in which economics has become as important as armies, investment as influential as ideology, and mutual dependence more decisive than old narratives of leadership.
The real significance of Cairo’s offer is therefore not military at all.
It is historical.
For the first time in modern Arab politics, the region’s traditional center of political gravity is openly acknowledging that its own security and prosperity are inseparable from the stability of the Gulf. And in that admission lies one of the most consequential geopolitical shifts the Arab world has witnessed since the end of the Cold War.
