articles.title: Are Lebanese Shi'ites abandoning Hezbollah? Poll shows majority favor disarming group - analysis
articles.body:
Hezbollah may face growing criticism from within Lebanon's Shi’ite community, which has formed the backbone of its support for decades, according to a report from KAN on Saturday.
A recent survey of Shi’ites got attention in regional media. As reported by Israel's KAN public broadcaster and the Lebanese Kataeb.org website, the survey, whose results emerged in mid-October, suggested that many Shi'ites are increasingly questioning the terrorist group.
The main question is whether Hezbollah should keep its arsenal. People also questioned Hezbollah’s conduct in the wars with Israel. However, this did not necessarily mean that Hezbollah is losing its influence over the community.
Respondents said decisions regarding war and peace should be left to the Lebanese state
The survey, conducted by Statistics Lebanon in September among 800 Lebanese Shi'ites, found that 66.4% supported transferring Hezbollah's weapons to the Lebanese state. Another 29.6% preferred that the terrorist organization retain its weapons. The results were significant because Hezbollah has argued that its arsenal is essential for defending Lebanon against Israel.
Roi Kais at Israel’s KAN noted, “A new survey has revealed that about 66 percent of Lebanese Shi'ites support Hezbollah's transfer of weapons to the state, and more than 40 percent express anger and disappointment with its leadership. Amid growing criticism, the support networks and status the terrorist organization has given the sect still maintain its power - as long as no other entity fills the vacuum.”
Notably, Kataeb.org, the website of the Phalange Party (Kataeb Party), a political party in Lebanon, published details on the survey. The Christian Kataeb Party opposes Hezbollah. The website noted that 71.1% of respondents believed that decisions about war and peace should rest exclusively with the Lebanese state. Only 5.9% believed Hezbollah's leadership should have a greater role in determining Lebanon's future.
Only 16.5% of respondents had confidence in Hezbollah's ability to guarantee security
The survey also revealed considerable confidence in the Lebanese Armed Forces. Some 78.5% expressed trust in the army, while 51.1% identified it as the institution best suited to guarantee long-term security. Only 16.5% selected Hezbollah.
These findings raised questions about Hezbollah's traditional claim to represent the security interests of Lebanon's Shi'ites. They suggested that many within the community may prefer stronger state institutions, even if they continue to identify politically or socially with Hezbollah.
The survey also found that 67.4% believed Hezbollah had either failed to achieve its objectives in the war with Israel or had achieved only some of them. Another 42.1% expressed disappointment, anger or concern about Hezbollah's leadership and the consequences of the conflict. Nevertheless, 59.5% continued to express varying degrees of trust in Hezbollah, including 37.1% who reported a great deal of trust.
An earlier survey presented a very different picture. In a June 10 analysis published by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), researchers Orna Mizrahi and Moran Levanoni cited a May 2026 survey by Lebanon's Information International in which 87.5% of Shiite respondents opposed disarming Hezbollah, while only 7.9% supported surrendering its weapons. More than 90% opposed ties with Israel.
The contrast with the September findings led to many questions. How can people hold such different views? Is it possible that some of the surveys are biased in their questions or agendas?
Mizrahi and Levanoni argued that Hezbollah's influence rests on its social and economic networks, political power, and the historical marginalization of Lebanon's Shi'ites.
They also noted that intimidation has discouraged opposition within the Shi’ite community. The researchers suggested that weakening Hezbollah's influence would require a stronger Lebanese army and Western and Gulf financial assistance to enable the state to replace Hezbollah's services.
This illustrated the complex relationship between Hezbollah and Lebanon's Shi'ites. Hezbollah is not just a terrorist group. It built networks of social services, financial institutions, and political influence to hedge its bets and take over the Lebanese state.
Now that it is so powerful, it is hard to uproot. Many people in Lebanon feared opposing Hezbollah over the years. For some Shi’ite families, it remains an important source of employment and assistance, even if they have to sacrifice their security due to the wars that Hezbollah has caused.
Lebanese fear Hezbollah-linked facilities could become Israeli targets
KAN highlighted an example from the southern Lebanese city of Tyre, where property owners reportedly opposed opening a branch of Hezbollah-linked financial institution Al-Qard Al-Hassan in their building. They feared the branch could become a target for Israeli strikes. The branches have been targeted in the past.
Hezbollah is attempting to regain support through reconstruction assistance. According to KAN, Hezbollah recently announced aid of up to $14,000 for eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs whose primary homes were destroyed, and up to $12,000 elsewhere.
The broader question is whether dissatisfaction will translate into political change. Hezbollah has suffered significant military and leadership losses since the war began, including the killing of Hassan Nasrallah in September 2024.
Yet its influence is rooted in decades of political and social organization. Lebanon did not jump at the opportunity to uproot the group in 2025. In March 2026, a new war broke out, leading to massive destruction of villages in southern Lebanon. Even today, Beirut moves at a snail’s pace.
The survey suggests that support for Hezbollah's terrorist role may be weakening even among its traditional constituency. However, unless the Lebanese state can provide security, reconstruction, and economic opportunities, the criticism won’t lead to major change.

articles.title: Investment security key to global gas market stability
articles.body:
According to Iranian oil ministry's news service-SHANA, in an interview, Ali-Mohammad Mousavi, deputy oil minister for international affairs and trade and Iran’s representative at international energy forums, discussed the Moscow summit’s objectives, Iran’s agenda, the GECF’s role in global energy governance and opportunities for advancing Iran’s gas diplomacy.
Q: What are the circumstances surrounding the eighth GECF summit, and how do you assess its significance?
Mousavi: The eighth GECF summit is taking place at a critical juncture in the evolution of the international energy system and coincides with the forum’s 25th anniversary. In recent years, the global natural gas market has undergone significant changes driven by geopolitical, economic, technological and environmental factors.
Changes in international gas trade patterns, the expansion of liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure, growing concerns over supply and demand security, intensifying competition for investment and rising energy needs in emerging economies have underscored the importance of dialogue and coordination among gas-producing and exporting countries.
Against this backdrop, the summit provides an opportunity for leaders to exchange views at the highest political level, assess long-term market trends and strengthen common approaches to strategic issues facing the natural gas industry.
The significance of the summit extends beyond reviewing market developments. It can also help reinforce the GECF’s position as an influential platform for international energy dialogue and for safeguarding the legitimate interests of gas-producing and exporting countries.
Q: What level of participation will Iran have at the Moscow summit, and what is planned for the Iranian delegation?
Mousavi: Iran was the principal proponent of establishing the GECF and is one of its founding members. As a country with some of the world’s largest proven natural gas reserves, Iran has consistently played an active and influential role in the forum’s activities.
At the eighth summit, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will lead a high-level delegation accompanied by Hamid Bovard, caretaker oil minister.
The president’s address to the summit, outlining Iran’s principled positions on international developments and the global energy market, as well as the country’s views on the future of gas cooperation, will be among the main events of the visit.
Before the leaders’ summit, the forum’s 28th ministerial meeting will bring together ministers and senior representatives of member countries. The meeting will review and approve the secretariat’s programs and finalize the documents to be presented to the summit.
The Iranian delegation also plans to hold bilateral meetings with senior officials from member and observer countries, particularly on energy cooperation. Discussions will explore opportunities to expand bilateral and multilateral ties in natural gas trade, investment, infrastructure development, technology transfer, technological cooperation and the use of shared capacities among member countries.
Q: What are Iran’s main priorities and positions at the eighth summit?
Mousavi: Iran’s positions can be outlined along two principal dimensions: political issues and strategic energy priorities.
On the political front, one of the Iranian delegation’s priorities will be to explain the dimensions of the military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran and condemn actions targeting the country’s national sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.
In this context, the martyrdom of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, military commanders and civilians, as well as events related to Minab and Lamerd, will be addressed in line with Iran’s official positions.
In the energy sector, our key priorities include protecting the collective interests of forum members, strengthening the role of natural gas in energy security, ensuring continued investment across the gas value chain, countering unilateral restrictive measures against producers, and expanding technical, commercial and investment cooperation.
We believe energy security is a balanced, multidimensional concept. Achieving it requires simultaneous attention to security of supply for consumers, security of demand for producers, investment security and the sustainability of energy trade flows.
Q: Given recent geopolitical developments, how do you view the relationship between political stability and security in the global gas market?
Mousavi: Because the natural gas industry is capital-intensive, involves long investment recovery periods and depends on extensive production, transmission, processing and export infrastructure, it requires political stability, investment security and predictable market conditions more than many other economic activities.
Any escalation in geopolitical tensions, threats to energy infrastructure, disruption of transportation routes or imposition of unilateral restrictions can affect project financing costs, investment risks and energy prices, ultimately undermining supply security in regional and global markets.
For this reason, we emphasize the need to prevent the politicization of energy trade and its use as an instrument in international relations. I believe the global gas market should develop on the basis of cooperation, mutual benefit, respect for contractual obligations and nondiscriminatory access to technology, equipment and financial resources.
Energy security is a shared responsibility among producers, consumers and countries through which energy is transported. None of these stakeholders can guarantee lasting energy security without taking the interests and concerns of the others into account.
Q: How do you assess the role of natural gas in the global energy mix in the years ahead?
Mousavi: Given its technical, economic and environmental characteristics, natural gas will remain an important pillar of global energy supply in the coming decades.
Compared with coal, natural gas emits less carbon dioxide when burned to produce the same amount of energy. If methane emissions across the supply chain are effectively managed, it can also help reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
In addition, the flexibility of gas-fired power plants allows them to support the integration of intermittent renewable energy sources, including solar and wind power.
Population growth, industrial development, urbanization and rising electricity demand in developing countries also provide considerable scope for natural gas to maintain its role in the global energy mix.
However, energy transition pathways differ from one country to another. Energy policies must reflect each country’s economic conditions, level of development, resource base and national priorities.
At the Oil Ministry, we believe the energy transition should be realistic, equitable and based on diversifying energy sources. It should not lead to unreasonable restrictions on investment in the natural gas industry.
Q: The GECF has emphasized the need for investment in the gas industry. Why is this important?
Mousavi: The sustainable development of the natural gas industry requires continuous, long-term investment across the entire value chain, from exploration and field development to processing, transmission, storage, exports and LNG infrastructure.
Because major gas projects generally require substantial financial resources and long periods for design, construction and operation, a stable and predictable investment environment is particularly important.
Reduced or delayed upstream investment can constrain supply capacity over the medium and long term, intensify price volatility and increase the vulnerability of the global gas market. Such an outcome would benefit neither producers nor consumers.
Accordingly, one of Iran’s key messages at the Moscow summit will be the need to strike a balance among energy security objectives, economic development and environmental considerations.
Producer countries must have fair access to financial resources, advanced technologies and consumer markets. Political barriers and unilateral restrictions should not obstruct the development of natural gas production and export capacity.
Q: What role does the GECF play in developments in the global gas market, and can it be considered an organization similar to OPEC?
Mousavi: The GECF is an intergovernmental organization with a consultative, analytical and cooperative mandate. It was established to strengthen engagement among natural gas-producing and exporting countries.
Unlike OPEC, the GECF does not have a mechanism for setting production quotas or directly managing natural gas supply volumes in the global market.
Structural differences between oil and gas markets, including the significant role of long-term contracts in gas trade, dedicated transmission infrastructure and the regional characteristics of gas markets, mean that cooperation within the forum operates differently.
Nevertheless, the GECF can play an effective role in strengthening natural gas’s position and defending producers’ shared interests by facilitating the exchange of views, experience and information; conducting specialized studies; providing long-term market outlooks; promoting technical cooperation; and coordinating members’ positions in international forums.
Strengthening the secretariat’s technical and research capabilities, expanding technological cooperation and increasing the forum’s participation in global energy discussions can further enhance its role in international energy governance.
Q: What capacity does Iran have to expand gas cooperation with other GECF members?
Mousavi: Thanks to its vast natural gas reserves, strategic geographical position, extensive gas transmission network, long experience in developing and operating gas fields, and technical and engineering capabilities, Iran has considerable potential to expand regional and international cooperation.
Iran’s geographical position, connecting energy-rich regions with consumer markets, offers opportunities to develop regional gas trade and transit cooperation.
Potential areas of cooperation with GECF members include expanding gas exports through pipelines and LNG, establishing swap and transit arrangements, cooperating in field development, participating in processing and infrastructure projects, and exchanging technical expertise.
Cooperation in reservoir management, improving recovery rates, reducing gas flaring, optimizing energy consumption, cutting methane emissions and developing technologies across the gas value chain could also become part of specialized engagement among member countries.
Realizing this potential will require political will among member countries, favorable economic, technical, contractual and investment conditions, and arrangements that ensure mutual benefits for all parties involved.
MNA

articles.title: Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price
articles.body:
Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price
With Americans struggling from soaring energy prices, and businesses across the country trying to keep their heads above water, the Democrats’ apparent priority is to threaten companies that might help ease the pressure.
According to an October 22 Washington Post report, Senate Democrats are preparing to investigate American companies involved in US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee has reportedly asked businesses to preserve relevant documents ahead of possible congressional investigations, should Democrats regain control of Congress in the November midterms.
For a party that claims to champion working Americans, this is a peculiar way of demonstrating its concern.
Diesel is the lifeblood of the American economy. It powers the trucks that carry food to supermarkets, the tractors that harvest crops, the machinery that builds homes and roads, and the locomotives that move freight across the vast country.
Yet the people who depend on it have too often been treated as an afterthought by the Washington establishment. They live and work in the industrial towns, farming communities and sprawling rural counties that coastal political elites dismiss as flyover country.
Just recall Hillary Clinton’s infamous 2016 description of millions of Trump supporters as a “basket of deplorables” – a perfect crystallization of the contempt that many ordinary Americans felt was directed at them by the Democrats.
A decade later, that perception is unlikely to be helped by the Democratic lawmakers’ threats to investigate businesses for participating in an arrangement intended to bring additional fuel to the market.
The timing makes those threats extra galling. America is facing an energy crunch aggravated by the Trump administration’s own military campaign against Iran. There is no reason to pretend otherwise. Yes, the president’s decisions helped disrupt global energy markets, and Americans are entitled to demand answers about their consequences.
But recognizing that responsibility does not mean opposing every subsequent attempt to alleviate the damage.
Trump’s decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel represents an effort to increase available supplies at a time when the market desperately needs relief. It is a pragmatic response to an immediate economic problem, whatever one thinks of the circumstances that created it.
And now Democrats are determined to make that response costly for the companies willing to participate.
Congress has every right to examine whether the administration acted within its legal authority. But threatening private businesses with investigations for engaging in transactions authorized by the federal government is another matter entirely. If those companies comply with the law, why should they have to fear becoming targets of a future congressional majority?
The actual volume of Russian diesel involved is almost beside the point. Moscow initially pledged to release some 300,000 metric tons of diesel, with further shipments promised in the following months – a modest quantity compared to America’s enormous fuel consumption.
But that’s not what the markets will be reacting to. They react to expectations, regulatory certainty and the willingness of businesses to undertake transactions without fearing political retaliation. And now, even a lawful, government-authorized energy deal could expose companies to years of investigations simply because a different party took power.
Just imagine the chilling effect.
Today, the dispute concerns a relatively small quantity of fuel from one supplier. Tomorrow, the same approach could be applied to other commodities, trading partners or commercial arrangements that fall afoul of Washington’s shifting ideological priorities.
In effect, the Democrats want to hold American energy security hostage to domestic political warfare.
And for what? The ostensible objective is to keep pressuring Russia.
For years, Moscow has faced sweeping Western sanctions, restrictions on financial transactions and efforts to shut its energy exports out of international markets. None of this has forced Russia to accept any of the West’s demands.
Russia has shown it can adapt and endure economic pressure. While not entirely painless, sanctions have consistently failed to produce the political outcome their advocates have called and hoped for.
Meanwhile, Moscow has repeatedly signaled that it remains prepared to negotiate to reasonable counterparts that would take Russia’s own security concerns and national interests into account. Whether those positions are acceptable to Washington is a matter for diplomacy – and refusing to talk altogether is not diplomacy.
Trump is willing to acknowledge that Russia remains a major power with which the US must eventually find a workable relationship. It’s the baseline level of recognition of political reality one expects from the leader of a major world power.
What the Democrats are doing is the international-politics equivalent of pressing their hands to their ears and shouting ‘La La La’ at the top of their lungs.
The truck driver paying more at the pump, the farmer counting operating costs for the next season and the small-business owner watching expenses climb have little interest in Washington’s political theater. They want affordable fuel, predictable costs and a government that remembers whom it is supposed to serve.
Threatening investigations to discourage companies from helping supply the American market is not sending the message the Democrats seem to think it’s sending. It suggests that, to them, political obedience matters more than keeping the country running.
And ordinary Americans could once again be left paying the bill.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: South Korea proposes military talks with North Korea to ease tensions along border
articles.body:
South Korea proposes military talks with North Korea to ease tensions along border
South Korea renewed its offer Friday to hold military talks with North Korea to discuss their conflicting views on where the inter-Korean border sits, seeking to ease tensions sparked by last month's land mine blast inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), Yonhap reported.
"Different perceptions remain over the Military Demarcation Line (MDL)," Deputy Defense Minister Kim Hong-cheol said in a press briefing, referring to the border separating the two Koreas.
"South Korea's Defense Ministry hereby officially proposes holding inter-Korean military talks with North Korean authorities to jointly verify the locations of the land-based MDL, restore military communication lines and discuss measures to prevent accidental clashes along the border," he said.
Kim said trilateral dialogue involving the U.N. Command (UNC), which administers and enforces the Armistice Agreement governing the border area, can also be considered.
Seoul and Pyongyang have traded sharp rhetoric since South Korea blamed the North for the Sept. 21 mine blast inside the DMZ that injured three South Korean troops. Pyongyang has denied responsibility and vowed to take military actions along the border if needed.
The latest escalation of tensions comes amid Seoul's suspicions that North Korean forces have repeatedly crossed the MDL to carry out border fortification work, such as erecting fences and laying mines, in potential violation of the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
Earlier, South Korea voiced concern over North Korea heightening border tensions with threats.

articles.title: Spain tests new anti-drone systems at army exercise
articles.body:
- EM&E Group used remote weapon stations on 4x4 and 6x6 vehicles and a jamming robot to down drones at Spain’s ATLAS 26 exercise.
- The systems were shown as configurations of ARACNE, the counter-drone system EM&E is developing with Indra for the Spanish Armed Forces.
Spanish defense company EM&E Group used remote weapon stations on armored vehicles and a jamming-equipped ground robot to detect and shoot down several drones during the Spanish military’s ATLAS 26 counter-drone exercise this week at the Médano del Loro firing range in Huelva, in southwestern Spain.
The exercise was led by Spain’s Chief of the Defence Staff, organized by the Maneuver Support Command and directed by the Spanish Army’s Anti-Aircraft Artillery Command. EM&E, formerly known as Escribano Mechanical & Engineering, said it took part with several configurations of ARACNE, the counter-drone system it is developing with Indra Group through a joint venture.
Two 4×4 tactical vehicles took part fitted with EM&E’s GUARDIAN 2.0 remote weapon station as a hard-kill option, meaning they physically destroy drones with gunfire instead of disrupting them electronically. The company also fielded its FEROX 6×6 armored vehicle carrying the GUARDIAN L-HIT remote station, which it uses to both detect and engage drones, and deployed its AUNAV LINK robotic vehicle with an integrated electronic warfare package that jams the radio links between a drone and its operator to block or distort its communications.
EM&E said the systems detected and shot down several drones during the exercise, without giving numbers or details of the targets.
ARACNE is one of the Spanish Armed Forces’ main counter-drone programs. The roughly 30.24 million euro ($34 million) effort covers 14 systems for the military, seven fixed and seven mobile, intended to protect critical infrastructure and military convoys, with mobile versions mounted on Vamtac ST5 tactical vehicles. The system pairs Indra’s sensors and command software with EM&E hardware, including a SmartEar radio-frequency scanner that monitors frequencies from 400 MHz to 6 GHz within about 6 km (3.7 miles) and an EM&E electro-optical station that can spot targets more than 14 km (8.7 miles) away with its daylight camera and up to 23.1 km (14.4 miles) with its thermal channel.
Indra and EM&E also demonstrated ARACNE at last year’s ATLAS 25 exercise, held at the same Huelva range from Oct. 20 to 24, 2025, where Indra said the system’s command and control software stood out for its ability to combine data from its own sensors and third-party sensors. A counter-drone system that Indra continues to develop under the ARACNE project also protects the Spanish contingent deployed with NATO in Lithuania, and Indra said in March 2026 that it had drawn interest from several countries on the alliance’s eastern flank.
The ATLAS exercises bring together Spanish military units and industry to test systems for detecting, identifying and defeating drones, and EM&E’s demonstrations this year added ground robotics and electronic warfare to the gun-based options shown on its vehicles.

articles.title: Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
articles.body:
Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
Kiev has moved to block a planned tribute to Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich, who was involved in the killing of an estimated 100,000 Poles during World War II ethnic purges, officials in Warsaw have claimed.
The reported retreat comes amid a series of disputes between the two countries in recent months over Kiev’s veneration of Nazi-linked figures that have eroded Polish support for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.
The controversy erupted on Tuesday when the Lviv Regional Council in western Ukraine voted to declare 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and to celebrate the 120th anniversary of its commander Roman Shukhevich while deciding to organize “cultural, memorial, scientific, and mass media events,” as well as exhibitions and national patriotic rallies on the occasion.
The move triggered a fierce response in Poland, which regards the UPA as perpetrators of genocide against Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia and Shukhevich as a key “architect” of the massacres. Before becoming a UPA leader, Shukhevich served in Nazi Germany’s Nachtigall Battalion and the German-controlled 201st Schutzmannschaft Battalion, which operated in occupied Belarus.
On Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk condemned the resolution as “unwise” and “suicidal tactics,” saying it “harms Ukraine,” while Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called the move “unacceptable,” warning that it would deepen divisions between the neighboring countries. Meanwhile, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski called for the resolution’s key sponsor, Lviv regional lawmaker Svyatoslav Sheremeta, to be put on a list of individuals deemed undesirable in Poland.
Following the backlash, Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said on Wednesday that officials of Vladimir Zelensky’s office had assured Warsaw that the controversial resolutions would not come into force. On Friday, Tusk echoed the claim, saying that Zelensky had personally signaled he would not endorse the resolution, adding that the Ukrainian leader was “unhappy” with the situation.
This also came after the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry called the Shukhevich tribute in Lviv “counterproductive to our current efforts aimed at further developing Ukrainian-Polish relations.” The ministry stressed that the local authorities had sought no advice from government bodies to assess the consequences of their actions.
An unnamed source in Zelensky’s office cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda went so far as to describe the decision as a “catastrophe.” “Ukraine looks erratic. We have just resolved the previous crisis – and now this,” the source said, accusing regional officials of pursuing “cheap one-day hype” despite knowing all too well what the resolution would lead to.
While senior Ukrainian officials apparently distanced themselves from the controversy, the Lviv council’s original announcement remains accessible as of Saturday. Sheremet also previously defended the resolution, saying “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honor their memory.”
The dispute is the latest in a series of heated clashes between Kiev and Warsaw over Ukraine’s continued veneration of nationalist figures that collaborated with Nazi Germany during World War II.
In May, Zelensky awarded an elite Ukrainian special operations unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA,” prompting another diplomatic uproar, with Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripping the Ukrainian leader of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state decoration.

articles.title: Kadena Implements Curfew, Alcohol Restrictions for Junior Troops After Japanese Civilian Dies
articles.body:
The top Air Force commander on the Japanese island of Okinawa has clamped down alcohol and issued a curfew for junior enlisted Airmen and Guardians at Kadena Air Base for the next month. The order came roughly two weeks after a U.S. Marine was arrested for allegedly robbing and murdering a Japanese woman on the island.
Brig. Gen. John B. Gallemore, commander of the 18th Wing at Kadena, issued the Oct. 22 memo, ordering the “Curtailment of Liberty and the Consumption of Alcohol,” according to a memo posted on the popular unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page.
A PACAF spokesperson confirmed the memo’s authenticity. The order went into effect Oct. 22 and will last “throughout the 30-day period of reflection,” concluding on Nov. 8, according to the memo:
- All personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4 are not to consume alcohol.
- Off-base liberty between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. local time is curtailed for all personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4.
- Possession of alcohol is banned in all dormitories within Kadena Air Base, to include dormitory common areas.
During the period, “commanders at all levels are authorized to conduct unannounced, systematic health and welfare inspections of dormitory rooms to ensure compliance of this order,” the memo states.
The memo follows an Oct. 6 memo from United States Forces Japan that ordered similar liberty restrictions and personal conduct training as part of a “period of reflection” following the Marine’s arrest in connection with the alleged murder of an Okinawan woman in Naha.
Japanese police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, on Oct. 4 for allegedly killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi and stealing her wallet, Marine Corps Times reported.
“Incidents like this demand we pause for reflection,” Benjamin T. Watson, area coordinator for U.S. Forces Japan, wrote in the memo. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will continue to ensure full cooperation with Japanese authorities throughout the investigation.”
Watson added that serving on Okinawa “comes with responsibility.”
“We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home,” Watson wrote. “Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region.”
The USFJ memo prohibited alcohol consumption for 48 hours from Oct. 7-9 but stopped short of restricting consumption during the 30-day period of reflection. In a statement, PACAF Gallemore’s Oct. 22 memo contains extra restrictions.
“The 18th Wing continually assesses measures to reinforce good order and discipline and maintain positive relationships with our host community,” the PACAF statement read. “As part of the ongoing 30-day period of reflection on Okinawa, Japan, [Gallemore] determined that additional preventive measures were appropriate to reinforce expectations for responsible conduct among service members.”
Periods of reflection and associated restrictions have been used by commanders on Okinawa in the past to reinforce discipline after violent, criminal incidents involving U.S. personnel and Japanese residents. In 2024, USFJ prohibited all American troops in the country from publicly consuming alcohol from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. every day after a string of alleged sexual assaults. In 2017, the command prohibited all drinking and cut off-base liberty for troops on Okinawa after a fatal car crash involving a drunk Marine. In 2010, then-Brig. Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach—now the Chief of Staff—instituted a brief period of reflection restricting alcohol and off-base liberty at Kadena after a string of alcohol-related arrests. In 2008, commanders imposed the measure to calm an uproar in the surrounding community over allegations that a Marine raped a 14-year-old girl on the island, The Guardian reported.
Kadena is the closest U.S. air base to Taiwan, making it a strategically vital location should China ever launch an invasion.

articles.title: Army seeks new ways to power troops on the battlefield
articles.body:
UK Defence Innovation has opened a Tactical Power Challenge worth £2.45 million seeking better ways to generate, store, distribute and manage electrical power for deployed forces, run on behalf of the British Army with support from the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, according to UK Defence Innovation.
The competition is being delivered in partnership with Australia’s Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator and closes at noon on 10 November. Further detail is available on the government’s competition page.
The organisation said the challenge seeks innovative solutions to improve the generation, storage, distribution and management of electrical power for deployed forces.
Power has become one of the quieter constraints on how the Army fights. A dismounted section now carries radios, electronic warfare detectors, night vision, counter-drone equipment, tablets and the batteries for all of it, and the weight of those batteries competes directly with water and ammunition. At formation level the problem scales up into generators, fuel convoys and the thermal and acoustic signature that a diesel generator park produces for anyone looking.
Ukraine has made the point sharply over the past four years, because units operating dispersed and under constant observation cannot run a visible generator, and the fuel resupply that a traditional headquarters depends on is one of the easiest things for a drone operator to find and hit. Silent generation, solar and battery hybrids, and power management that lets one source feed several systems have all moved from convenience to survivability.
The Australian partnership places the competition inside a wider pattern of British and Australian innovation work, with the Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator performing a similar function to UK Defence Innovation. Running a challenge jointly gives a successful supplier two potential customers and gives both armies a chance of fielding compatible equipment, which matters more as the two countries work together under AUKUS Pillar Two on autonomy, artificial intelligence and electronic warfare.
UK Defence Innovation was established to replace the Defence and Security Accelerator and to put a single organisation in charge of pulling new technology into the department at pace, with a budget ringfenced under the Strategic Defence Review. Competitions of this kind are its main instrument, offering a defined sum against a defined problem on a short timetable.
